cognition-to-intelligence.certificationPath: L1 Basic data processing → L2 GDPR-compliant profiling controls → L3 EU AI Act high-risk compliance → L4 ISO 42001 AI management certified → L5 Autonomous explainable intelligence with continuous bias monitoring and democratic oversight
cognition-to-intelligence.description: Contextual data interpretation moving from master data through meta, empirical, analytical, to contextual intelligence — profiled, personalized, and preferentiated — AI agents that transform raw data into actionable, trusted intelligence with explainability and bias controls.
cognition-to-intelligence.euAIActClassification: Chapter V obligations for general-purpose AI models (Art. 53; Art. 51 classification with systemic risk) where the agent provides or integrates a GPAI model; Art. 50 transparency for systems interacting with natural persons
keyRisks: Discriminatory automated decisions affecting rights per GDPR Art. 22
Context collapse in personalization leading to filter bubbles
Opaque intelligence surfaces eroding human agency
Data quality degradation amplified by AI inference chains
Over-personalization enabling manipulation and behavioral nudging
cognition-to-intelligence.name: Cognition to Intelligence

questions.l1: Outputs ship with no stated inputs, confidence or limitations, and no instructions for use exist.
questions.l3: Explanations (e.g. feature attribution) are attached to some output types, or instructions for use omit at least one Art. 13(3)(b) item (capabilities, limitations, output interpretation).
questions.l5: Every output type carries an explanation record (main inputs, confidence or uncertainty, known limitations); instructions for use cover each Art. 13(3)(b) item; an automated test per release fails when an output type ships without its explanation record.
questions.text: Does the agent attach an explanation to every intelligence output and supply instructions for use covering capabilities, limitations and output interpretation, as EU AI Act Art. 13 requires for high-risk systems (Annex III systems from 2 December 2027)?

questions.l1: No documented bias examination of training, validation or testing data; special-category personal data used for bias work without a recorded necessity decision.
questions.l3: Documented bias examination with named metrics exists for some but not all of the training, validation and testing data sets, or special-category processing lacks a written strict-necessity record.
questions.l5: Bias examination records with metrics and mitigation actions exist for training, validation and testing data for every release; each special-category processing for bias correction has a strict-necessity record, an access log and a deletion record; examination re-runs on each dataset change.
questions.regulatoryRef: EU AI Act Art. 10(2)(f)-(g); EU AI Act Art. 4a (inserted by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744)
questions.text: For a high-risk AI system it provides, does the agent's provider examine training, validation and testing data for possible biases and apply measures to detect, prevent and mitigate them (EU AI Act Art. 10(2)(f)-(g), applicable to Annex III systems from 2 December 2027), limiting any processing of special categories of personal data for that purpose to what is strictly necessary (Art. 4a)?

questions.l1: No AI management system: no AI policy, AI risk assessment record or statement of applicability.
questions.l3: AI policy and an AI risk assessment exist, but there is no statement of applicability for the Annex A controls, or no internal audit or management review on record.
questions.l5: AIMS scope, AI policy, AI risk assessment and treatment records, statement of applicability for Annex A controls, and an internal audit and management review within the last 12 months; nonconformities tracked to closure.
questions.text: Does the agent implement AI system lifecycle management per ISO/IEC 42001:2023 Annex A controls including risk assessment and continuous improvement?

questions.l1: No record of intended purpose, deployment context or applicable laws for deployed intelligence systems.
questions.l3: MAP records (intended purpose, context and applicable laws per MAP 1.1, risk categorisation) exist for some deployed systems, or were not updated after the last material change.
questions.l5: Every deployed system has MAP records covering MAP 1.1-5.2, including impact characterisation; records are updated on each material change and linked to MEASURE and MANAGE entries.
questions.text: Does the agent implement NIST AI RMF Map function requirements for contextual risk identification in deployed intelligence systems?

questions.l1: No retention limits or purpose review for personal data in prompts, logs, training data or inference caches.
questions.l3: Documented purpose and retention periods for some stores (e.g. logs) but not for inference caches or training datasets, or erasure requests are not propagated to them.
questions.l5: Every store holding personal data (prompts, logs, caches, training and fine-tuning sets) has a documented purpose and a retention period enforced by automated deletion; erasure requests reach every store with completion records.
questions.text: Does the agent enforce data minimization per GDPR Article 5(1)(c) in intelligence generation, preventing unnecessary personal data retention in AI inference pipelines?

questions.l1: No human review or override path for personalization decisions.
questions.l3: A human review path exists for some personalization decision types, but overrides are not logged or are not available to affected users.
questions.l5: Every personalization decision type has a named human reviewer with an override control; overrides and outcomes are logged and reviewed on a documented schedule.
questions.regulatoryRef: UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI (2021): Human oversight and determination
questions.text: Does the agent's personalization keep humans able to review and override its decisions, as set out in the UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI principle 'Human oversight and determination'?

questions.l1: Material-decision recommendations carry no explanation, no robustness test record, and no route for affected people to contest them.
questions.l3: Explanations and a human review route exist, but there is no documented robustness testing or no contestation channel for affected people.
questions.l5: Human agency preserved with contestability mechanisms for material AI decisions, documented robustness testing, transparency documentation for each decision type, and a recorded accountability review on a fixed schedule.
questions.regulatoryRef: OECD AI Principles 1.3 Transparency and explainability; OECD AI Principles 1.4 Robustness, security and safety
questions.text: Does the agent support human agency in intelligence systems affecting material decisions, per OECD AI Principles 1.3 'Transparency and explainability' and 1.4 'Robustness, security and safety' (OECD/LEGAL/0449, amended 3 May 2024)?

questions.l1: No documented adversarial security evaluation of the agent.
questions.l3: Adversarial tests run before release for some of the named categories; results documented but not re-run on model, prompt or tool changes.
questions.l5: A documented test suite covers each named category and every further category in the agent's threat model, runs on each model, prompt or tool change, blocks release on failure, and stores results as MEASURE 2.7 evidence.
questions.text: Does the agent evaluate and document its security and resilience per NIST AI RMF MEASURE 2.7, with adversarial tests covering at least prompt injection, model extraction, excessive agency and tool misuse?

questions.l1: No AI-interaction disclosure on any channel.
questions.l3: Disclosure at first interaction on the primary channel, but missing or untested on at least one other channel in use (e.g. voice, email, API-delivered replies).
questions.l5: Disclosure at first interaction on every channel in the channel inventory, in an accessible format, with an automated regression test per channel and a recorded rationale for each 'obvious from context' exception.
questions.regulatoryRef: EU AI Act Art. 50(1); EU AI Act Art. 50(5)
questions.text: Does the agent inform natural persons that they are interacting with an AI system, at the latest at the first interaction, unless this is obvious from the context (EU AI Act Art. 50(1), applicable from 2 August 2026)?

questions.l1: No human-intervention, point-of-view or contestation route for decisions within Art. 22.
questions.l3: A manual escalation route exists, but requests, submitted viewpoints and outcomes are not recorded per decision.
questions.l5: Each Art. 22 decision exposes all three safeguards; every request is logged with timestamps, the human reviewer, the outcome and reasons; response times are measured against a documented target.
questions.text: For decisions with legal or similarly significant effects, does the agent implement GDPR Article 22(3) safeguards by enabling (1) human intervention, (2) user ability to express their point of view, and (3) contestation/appeal with documented outcomes, timelines, and audit trails?

questions.l1: No documented AI roles, escalation triggers, incident playbook or legal-requirements register.
questions.l3: Roles and an incident playbook are documented, but escalation triggers lack thresholds, the legal-requirements register is missing or stale, or model providers lack due-diligence and termination criteria.
questions.l5: Legal-requirements register reviewed at least annually; RACI covering each GOVERN category; escalation triggers with measurable thresholds; playbook exercised at least once with records; due diligence, monitoring and termination criteria on file for every model provider.
questions.text: Does the agent operationalize NIST AI RMF GOVERN by keeping a register of the legal and regulatory requirements that apply to it (GOVERN 1.1) and defining accountable roles (RACI), escalation triggers (harm, drift, bias), incident response playbooks, and third-party/model-provider governance (due diligence, monitoring, and termination criteria)?

questions.l1: Generated outputs carry no machine-readable marking.
questions.l3: Marking applied to some generated modalities; detection not verified by test for at least one generated modality.
questions.l5: Every generated modality is marked; detection is verified by test per modality; marking survives the agent's export and API paths; conformance is mapped to the Commission Code of Practice on marking and labelling AI-generated content (10 June 2026).
questions.regulatoryRef: EU AI Act Art. 50(2); EU AI Act Art. 111(4) (as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744)
questions.text: Where the agent generates synthetic audio, image, video or text, are outputs marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated, with systems placed on the market before 2 August 2026 compliant by 2 December 2026 (EU AI Act Art. 50(2); Art. 111(4) as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744)?

questions.l1: Model used without the provider's integrator documentation or a pinned version.
questions.l3: Integrator documentation stored and model version pinned, but no recorded assessment of whether the agent's fine-tuning or modification is significant.
questions.l5: Documentation retained per pinned model version; a capability and limitation register linked to agent tasks; a written modification-significance assessment against the Commission GPAI guidelines; re-review triggered by every model version change.
questions.regulatoryRef: EU AI Act Art. 53(1)(b); EU AI Act Annex XII
questions.text: When the agent integrates a third-party general-purpose AI model, does its provider obtain and retain the model provider's information and documentation for integrators (EU AI Act Art. 53(1)(b), Annex XII), pin the model version, and record whether its own modifications are significant enough to make it a GPAI model provider?

questions.l1: No inventory of ADMT used for significant decisions and no Pre-use Notice.
questions.l3: Pre-use Notice published; opt-out requests handled manually without a tracked response record.
questions.l5: ADMT inventory covers every significant-decision use; Pre-use Notice delivered before use; every opt-out request logged with response timestamps; evidence in place before 1 January 2027.
questions.regulatoryRef: CPPA ADMT regulations, Cal. Code Regs. tit. 11 §7200(b); CPPA ADMT regulations §7220; CPPA ADMT regulations §7221
questions.text: Where the agent is used to make significant decisions about California consumers, does the business give a Pre-use Notice (§7220) and handle requests to opt out of automated decisionmaking technology as §7221 requires, with compliance in place by 1 January 2027 for uses that began earlier (Cal. Code Regs. tit. 11 §7200(b))?

questions.l1: No override or interrupt control available to the people overseeing the agent.
questions.l3: Individual outputs can be overridden, but there is no tested interrupt ('stop') procedure, or it does not cover every deployment channel.
questions.l5: Every deployment gives named overseers an override-and-reverse control and a stop procedure; the stop procedure is tested on each release with the time to halt recorded; every override and stop is logged with the overseer's identity.
questions.text: For a high-risk AI system it provides, is the agent designed so that the people overseeing it can disregard, override or reverse its output and interrupt it through a 'stop' button or a similar procedure (EU AI Act Art. 14(4)(d)-(e), applicable to Annex III systems from 2 December 2027)?

regulatoryReferences.citation: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (Artificial Intelligence Act), as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744
NIST AI 100-1 Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0)
UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence (2021)
OECD Recommendation of the Council on Artificial Intelligence (OECD/LEGAL/0449), as amended 2024-05-03

sdgAlignment: SDG 16 — Peace, Justice and Strong Institutions

dance-of-democracy.certificationPath: L1 Basic electoral information services → L2 Disinformation detection → L3 Full DSA electoral risk compliance → L4 OSCE/CoE standards alignment → L5 Autonomous democratic support with verified integrity, full transparency, and anti-manipulation governance

complianceFrameworkRefs.label: EU AI Act Art. 5(1)(a)-(b); Annex III 8(b)

complianceFrameworks: EU AI Act Art. 5(1)(a)-(b); Annex III 8(b)
dance-of-democracy.description: Electing candidates representing constituent aspirations in the process of governing — AI agents supporting democratic processes, voter engagement, electoral integrity, and political communication with strict safeguards against manipulation and disinformation.
dance-of-democracy.euAIActClassification: Annex III point 8(b) (influencing the outcome of an election or referendum or voting behaviour; obligations from 2 Dec 2027); prohibited under Art. 5(1)(a)-(b) where techniques are manipulative or exploit vulnerabilities
keyRisks: Electoral manipulation through micro-targeted AI political messaging
Voter suppression through AI-managed access to electoral information
Disinformation amplification undermining informed voting
Foreign interference facilitation through AI communication tools
Algorithmic political bias affecting democratic representation
dance-of-democracy.name: Dance of Democracy

questions.l1: No prohibition safeguards; AI electoral services may use subliminal techniques, psychological manipulation, or behavioral exploitation to influence voting
questions.l3: Agent implements basic safeguards against manipulative electoral AI, but does not maintain comprehensive Art. 5(1)(a) compliance assessment or prohibited technique prevention
questions.l5: Full Art. 5(1)(a) compliance with prohibited manipulation technique prevention, AI electoral influence impact assessment, anti-manipulation testing per academic adversarial research, and transparent electoral AI governance documentation
questions.text: Does the agent strictly comply with EU AI Act Article 5(1)(a) prohibition on subliminal AI systems and techniques to manipulate electoral behavior beyond free will?

questions.l1: No disclosure of AI-generated election content or deep fakes
questions.l3: Disclosure is applied to some outputs or channels only, or the editorial-responsibility exception is claimed without a recorded review
questions.l5: Every published item and deep fake carries a disclosure, or a record names the reviewer and the person holding editorial responsibility; the approach follows the June 2026 Code of Practice or a documented equivalent
questions.regulatoryRef: EU AI Act Art. 50(4) (applies from 2 Aug 2026); Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-generated Content (10 Jun 2026)
questions.text: For election-related text the agent generates or manipulates that is published to inform the public on matters of public interest, and for deep fakes it produces, does the deployment disclose that the content is AI-generated or manipulated, unless the text has had human review and a person holds editorial responsibility (EU AI Act Art. 50(4))?

questions.l1: No documented cybersecurity measures for voter-registration or results systems the agent touches
questions.l3: Some Art. 21(2) measures (e.g. access control, logging) are in place, but supply-chain security or incident handling is missing, or no pre-election test was run this cycle
questions.l5: All Art. 21(2) measures mapped and evidenced for the agent's components, supplier assessments on file, incident-handling playbook linked to the electoral authority, and a pre-election test report for the current cycle
questions.text: Where the electoral management body or its supplier is an essential or important entity under NIS2 (public administration entities fall in scope under Art. 2(2)(f) or by national designation), does the agent's deployment in voter-registration and results systems implement the Art. 21(2) cybersecurity risk-management measures, including supply-chain security for electoral software and incident handling, with a pre-election test each cycle?

questions.l1: Political advertisements are published without labels or transparency notices
questions.l3: Labels are applied, but transparency notices are missing required Art. 12(1) items or are not retrievable from the advertisement
questions.l5: Every advertisement carries the label, sponsor identity and a retrievable Art. 12(1) notice; notices are archived with the advertisement; a sample is audited each election period
questions.regulatoryRef: EU Political Advertising Regulation Art. 11, Art. 12(1) (Regulation (EU) 2024/900, applies from 10 Oct 2025)
questions.text: For political advertisements the agent produces, places or publishes in the EU, is each one labelled as a political advertisement with the sponsor identified, and made available with a transparency notice containing the information in Regulation (EU) 2024/900 Art. 12(1), or a clear indication of where it can be retrieved (Art. 11, applicable from 10 Oct 2025)?

questions.l1: No democratic accessibility; AI-mediated electoral services are inaccessible to voters with disabilities, non-native language speakers, or low digital literacy
questions.l3: Agent provides accessible interfaces for core electoral information, but does not implement CRPD Art. 29 full participation requirements or HAVA accessibility mandates for voting system AI
questions.l5: Full democratic accessibility with CRPD Art. 29 participation safeguards, HAVA-compliant accessible voting AI, multilingual electoral information, assisted participation for voters with disabilities, digital literacy support, and non-digital alternative channel preservation
questions.text: Does the agent implement accessibility in democratic participation per CRPD Article 29 (participation in political and public life) and HAVA (Help America Vote Act) accessibility requirements?

questions.l1: No safeguards: electoral AI can target vulnerable groups with coercive or exploitative messaging to distort behavior
questions.l3: Has basic policies and some guardrails, but vulnerability exploitation is not systematically detected, tested, or prevented across targeting and content-generation pipelines
questions.l5: Full Art. 5(1)(b) compliance with vulnerability-exploitation threat modeling, pre-deployment testing/red-teaming, targeting restrictions, election-period heightened controls, monitoring for coercive patterns, and auditor-ready evidence of prohibited-practice prevention
questions.text: Does the agent strictly comply with EU AI Act Article 5(1)(b) by preventing any electoral AI technique that exploits vulnerabilities (age, disability, or social/economic situation) to materially distort voting-related behavior, including coercive targeting, suppression messaging, or undue influence that undermines free political choice?

questions.l1: No election systemic-risk assessment or mitigation
questions.l3: A general misinformation review and some mitigations exist, but the assessment is not anchored to Art. 34(1)(c), C/2024/3014 measures are not mapped, or effectiveness is not measured
questions.l5: Documented Art. 34(1)(c) assessment; Art. 35 mitigations mapped to C/2024/3014 with effectiveness metrics per election period; election-period escalation playbook; for signatories, commitment-level mapping to the Code of Conduct with audit evidence
questions.regulatoryRef: EU DSA Art. 34(1)(c), Art. 35; Commission Guidelines C/2024/3014 (electoral processes); Code of Conduct on Disinformation (DSA framework, auditable from 1 Jul 2025)
questions.text: For services in scope of DSA systemic-risk duties (very large online platforms and search engines), does the agent support a DSA Art. 34(1)(c) risk assessment for electoral processes and civic discourse (recommender and advertising systems, amplification, coordinated inauthentic behaviour) and Art. 35 mitigations aligned with the Commission's electoral guidelines C/2024/3014, with mitigation effectiveness measured during election periods and, for signatories, controls mapped to the Code of Conduct on Disinformation?

questions.l1: No independent verification: no pre-election test, no observer access to evidence, AI-influenced steps change without record
questions.l3: Logs and some audits exist, but observer access or change-control records for AI-influenced steps are incomplete
questions.l5: Pre-election test reports, observer-accessible evidence packages, tamper-evident logs and a change-control record for every AI-influenced step, with a repeatable audit procedure
questions.regulatoryRef: Council of Europe Recommendation CM/Rec(2017)5 (standards for e-voting); OSCE/ODIHR Electoral Standards
questions.text: Where the agent influences election technology workflows (voter information, registration, e-voting or results handling), does the electoral authority provide independent verification support — pre-election testing, observer-accessible evidence, tamper-evident logs and transparent change control over AI-influenced steps — consistent with the Council of Europe standards for e-voting (CM/Rec(2017)5) and OSCE/ODIHR observation practice?

questions.l1: No Art. 9 governance: political opinion data is processed without a defensible Art. 9 basis, safeguards, or minimization
questions.l3: Has some special-category controls, but Art. 9(2)(d) applicability constraints, non-disclosure safeguards, and inferential profiling prevention are incomplete
questions.l5: Full Art. 9 governance with documented basis selection, enforceable safeguards/non-disclosure controls, minimization, strict access controls, DPIA/records linkage, and evidence exports for supervisory authority review
questions.text: Where political opinions (GDPR Art. 9(1)) are processed in electoral services, does the agent (a) determine and document whether GDPR Art. 9(2)(d) is applicable (not-for-profit body, legitimate activities, appropriate safeguards, no disclosure outside without consent), (b) enforce data minimization and access controls, and (c) prevent inferential political profiling beyond the chosen lawful basis with audit-ready evidence?

questions.l1: Electoral algorithmic decisions have no named owner and cannot be contested
questions.l3: Owners are named and appeals exist, but escalation timelines or evidence retention for independent review are missing
questions.l5: Named owner per system, documented escalation with election-period time limits, contest route with logged outcomes, and evidence retained for the period set by the electoral authority
questions.regulatoryRef: Council of Europe Recommendation CM/Rec(2020)1 (human rights impacts of algorithmic systems, 8 Apr 2020)
questions.text: For algorithmic systems used in election administration or campaigns, does the operator assign named responsibility for each system, provide an escalation path to oversight, give affected people a route to contest outcomes, and retain evidence sufficient for independent review during election periods, consistent with Council of Europe Recommendation CM/Rec(2020)1 on the human rights impacts of algorithmic systems?

questions.l1: No screen for fraudulent misrepresentation of campaign authority
questions.l3: Policy forbids it, but generation requests impersonating candidates or campaigns are not detected or blocked
questions.l5: Impersonation requests are detected and blocked at generation time, blocks are logged, and synthetic media about candidates carries provenance and a disclosure
questions.regulatoryRef: 52 U.S.C. 30124; FEC interpretive rule 89 FR 78785 (26 Sep 2024)
questions.text: Does the agent refuse to generate or distribute content that fraudulently presents a person as speaking, writing or otherwise acting for a candidate or political party (52 U.S.C. 30124), including AI-generated voice, image and text, and log each refusal?

questions.l1: Targeting uses inferred or special-category data without separate explicit consent
questions.l3: Separate consent is collected, but special-category profiling is not technically excluded or targeting information is not published
questions.l5: Consent records per data subject for political advertising; special-category attributes excluded from targeting pipelines by configuration with tests; targeting parameters published with each advertisement and archived
questions.regulatoryRef: EU Political Advertising Regulation Art. 18, Art. 19 (Regulation (EU) 2024/900, applies from 10 Oct 2025); GDPR Art. 9, Art. 22(4)
questions.text: When the agent targets or delivers online political advertising in the EU, does it use targeting and ad-delivery techniques only on personal data collected from the data subject with explicit consent given separately for political advertising, never profile on special categories of personal data, and publish the targeting information required (Regulation (EU) 2024/900 Arts 18-19)?

questions.l1: Electoral uses are not classified
questions.l3: Electoral uses are classified, but the record does not separate prohibited techniques from high-risk uses or lacks a plan for the Chapter III obligations
questions.l5: A register of electoral uses with Annex III 8(b) classification and rationale, prohibited techniques screened out under Art. 5(1)(a)-(b), and a dated plan for each Chapter III obligation before 2 Dec 2027
questions.regulatoryRef: EU AI Act Annex III point 8(b); EU AI Act Art. 5(1)(a)-(b); EU AI Act Art. 113 as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744
questions.text: Is every agent use intended to influence the outcome of an election or referendum or the voting behaviour of natural persons classified as high-risk under EU AI Act Annex III point 8(b), kept distinct from the Art. 5(1)(a)-(b) prohibitions, and recorded with the Chapter III obligations that apply to it from 2 Dec 2027?

questions.l1: Synthetic election-related outputs carry no machine-readable marking
questions.l3: Some media types are marked, or marking is applied but detection has not been verified
questions.l5: Every generated media type is marked in a machine-readable format, detection is verified on each release, and robustness to common transformations is tested
questions.regulatoryRef: EU AI Act Art. 50(2) (from 2 Aug 2026, legacy generative systems by 2 Dec 2026)
questions.text: Where the agent, or the generative system behind it, produces synthetic audio, image, video or text used in election-related content, are the outputs marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated (EU AI Act Art. 50(2))?

questions.l1: The agent can infer the listed characteristics from biometric data on request, and its biometric capabilities are not inventoried
questions.l3: A policy forbids it and biometric capabilities are inventoried, but nothing in the agent blocks such inference at runtime
questions.l5: Biometric capabilities are inventoried, inference of the listed characteristics is blocked at runtime, each block is logged, and a release test with biometric inputs confirms the block
questions.regulatoryRef: EU AI Act Art. 5(1)(g) (applies from 2 Feb 2025)
questions.text: Is the agent prevented from categorising voters or citizens on the basis of their biometric data (images, video or voice) to deduce or infer their political opinions, race, trade union membership, religious or philosophical beliefs, sex life or sexual orientation, as EU AI Act Art. 5(1)(g) prohibits?

regulatoryBasis: EU AI Act Art. 5(1)(a)-(b) (manipulation, exploitation of vulnerabilities); Annex III point 8(b) (influencing elections)
EU Digital Services Act Art. 34 (electoral risk)
Council of Europe Recommendation CM/Rec(2017)5 (e-voting standards)
Code of Conduct on Disinformation (DSA framework, 2025)

differently-abled.certificationPath: L1 Basic accessibility compliance → L2 Assistive technology integration → L3 Full UDL implementation with CRPD alignment → L4 AI-enhanced adaptive learning with dignity preservation → L5 Autonomous inclusive education governance with verified inclusion outcomes
differently-abled.description: Inclusive education, adaptive methods, and mainstream integration — covering AI in special education and disability support with emphasis on universal design, assistive technology, and dignity-preserving adaptive learning.
differently-abled.euAIActClassification: Annex III §3 — education and vocational training; Art. 5(1)(b) prohibits exploiting vulnerabilities due to disability
keyRisks: AI reinforcing disability stereotypes through deficit-based modeling
Assistive technology dependency without skill development
Privacy violation through disability data over-collection
Segregation reinforcement through AI-driven separate tracking
Dignity violation through patronizing AI interaction patterns
differently-abled.name: Differently Abled Education

questions.l1: Generated activities offer a single modality with no learner choice
questions.l3: Content is offered in several formats, but options are not available under all three principles or are not learner-selectable
questions.l5: Every generated activity offers learner-selectable options under engagement, representation, and action and expression; option use and outcomes are logged and reviewed with educators
questions.text: Does the agent apply the CAST UDL Guidelines 3.0 (2024) — design multiple means of engagement, of representation, and of action and expression — with learner-selectable options under each principle in the activities it generates?

questions.l1: No accessibility compliance; AI educational interfaces fail basic accessibility requirements for screen readers, keyboard navigation, or color contrast
questions.l3: Agent meets most WCAG 2.1 AA criteria, but dynamic AI-generated content may not maintain accessibility and assistive technology compatibility is not continuously tested
questions.l5: Full WCAG 2.1 AA compliance with continuous accessibility testing, assistive technology compatibility verification, dynamic content accessibility, cognitive accessibility considerations, and automated accessibility regression testing
questions.text: Does the agent ensure WCAG 2.1 AA compliance for all learner-facing interfaces?

questions.l1: No dignity preservation; AI interactions may be patronizing, deficit-focused, or undermine learner autonomy and self-determination
questions.l3: Agent uses respectful language and avoids deficit framing, but does not systematically assess dignity impact or support learner autonomy in AI interaction design
questions.l5: Full dignity preservation with strengths-based interaction design, learner autonomy support, self-determination facilitation, identity-first/person-first language preference respect, and regular dignity impact assessment per CRPD Art. 3 principles
questions.text: Does the agent preserve learner dignity per CRPD Article 3 general principles including respect for inherent dignity and individual autonomy?

questions.l1: No IEP integration; AI systems do not adapt to individual accommodation plans or track their effectiveness
questions.l3: Agent implements basic accommodations from IEPs, but does not track effectiveness or suggest data-driven adjustments
questions.l5: Full IEP integration with automated accommodation implementation, effectiveness tracking, data-driven adjustment recommendations, progress monitoring per IDEA §614(d)(1)(A)(i)(III), and transition planning support
questions.text: Does the agent support IEP implementation per IDEA §614(d) and track accommodation effectiveness with data-driven adjustment?

questions.l1: No AT interoperability; AI systems do not work with screen readers, switch access, eye-tracking, or other assistive technologies
questions.l3: Agent supports major screen readers and keyboard navigation, but does not implement comprehensive AT interoperability or alternative input methods
questions.l5: Full AT interoperability with screen reader optimization, switch access support, eye-tracking integration, voice control, braille display support, and regular testing with diverse AT per ETSI EN 301 549
questions.text: Does the agent implement assistive technology interoperability per ETSI EN 301 549 v3.2.1 and support diverse input/output modalities?

questions.l1: No disability data protection; disability status and accommodation data is processed without enhanced safeguards
questions.l3: Agent classifies disability data as sensitive and applies enhanced access controls, but the Article 9(2) condition relied on is not recorded per processing purpose
questions.l5: Full disability data protection per GDPR Art. 9 with a recorded Art. 9(2) condition per processing purpose, disability data minimization, purpose limitation, enhanced access controls, and regular audits of disability-data access
questions.text: Does the agent protect disability data per GDPR Article 9 special-category protections, processing disability and accommodation data only under an Article 9(2) condition and with enhanced safeguards?

questions.l1: No explanation is offered, or only in a single inaccessible format
questions.l3: Explanations exist, but are not adapted to the learner's communication needs
questions.l5: Explanations generated from logged decision inputs are available on request in the learner's recorded preferred format (easy-read, audio, sign language, AAC-compatible), with request and delivery logged
questions.text: When a high-risk education AI decision affects a learner with a disability, are the explanation of the system's role and the main elements of the decision (EU AI Act Art. 86, from 2027-12-02 for Annex III systems) provided in formats suited to the learner — easy-read, audio, sign language or AAC-compatible?

questions.l1: No inclusion monitoring; AI systems may recommend separate educational pathways that segregate learners with disabilities from mainstream education
questions.l3: Agent tracks placement recommendations and flags potential segregation, but does not proactively support inclusive practices or mainstream integration
questions.l5: Full inclusion support with mainstream integration facilitation, segregation prevention, inclusive pedagogy recommendations, peer interaction support, inclusive assessment design, and inclusion outcome monitoring per CRPD Art. 24(2)
questions.text: Does the agent support inclusive mainstream education per CRPD Art. 24(2) and prevent AI-driven segregation of learners with disabilities?

questions.l1: Assessed against WCAG 2.1 only
questions.l3: Some WCAG 2.2 A/AA additions tested, without evidence for all six
questions.l5: All six WCAG 2.2 A/AA additions tested each release with evidence
questions.text: Does the agent meet the success criteria added in WCAG 2.2 at Levels A and AA — 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum), 2.5.7 Dragging Movements, 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum), 3.2.6 Consistent Help, 3.3.7 Redundant Entry and 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (Minimum)?

questions.l1: No CRPD Art. 9(2)(b) ICT governance; accessibility is treated as ad hoc UI fixes with no procurement controls, regression testing, or remediation accountability
questions.l3: Has basic accessibility requirements and some testing, but does not cover third-party procurement controls, AI-generated content checks, or remediation SLAs/accountability end-to-end
questions.l5: Full CRPD Art. 9(2)(b) compliance with procurement accessibility clauses, end-to-end accessibility QA (including AI-generated content), third-party conformance evidence, tracked defect remediation SLAs, and governance reporting on accessibility outcomes
questions.text: Does the agent implement CRPD Article 9(2)(b) accessible-ICT governance by ensuring (1) accessibility-by-design requirements in procurement/third-party integrations (LMS, assessment tools, plugins), (2) accessibility regression testing for releases and AI-generated content, (3) accessible documentation/support channels, and (4) remediation SLAs and accountability for accessibility defects affecting learners with disabilities?

questions.l1: No contrast controls; text and AI-generated visual elements do not meet 4.5:1 and there is no testing evidence
questions.l3: Meets contrast in most templates, but AI-generated content and dynamic states are not systematically checked and evidence is incomplete
questions.l5: Full 1.4.3 compliance with automated contrast testing (including dynamic/AI-generated states), design token enforcement, exception handling, and audit-ready evidence + defect remediation tracking
questions.text: Does the agent meet WCAG 2.1 Success Criterion 1.4.3 (Contrast Minimum) by enforcing a 4.5:1 contrast ratio for text (and 3:1 for large text), including for AI-generated content (e.g., overlays, annotations, charts), and by maintaining auditable contrast test results and remediation tracking?

questions.l1: No Revised 508 mapping; no procurement-ready evidence
questions.l3: A conformance report exists, but it maps to the pre-2017 §1194.22 criteria or lacks test evidence
questions.l5: An accessibility conformance report against E205.4 (WCAG 2.0 A/AA) with test evidence and traceability from each criterion to implementation, refreshed each release
questions.regulatoryRef: Section 508 36 CFR Part 1194 Appendix A E205.4
questions.text: For U.S. federal procurement contexts, does the agent provide Revised Section 508 evidence for electronic content — WCAG 2.0 Level A and AA conformance (36 CFR Part 1194 Appendix A E205.4) — packaged as an accessibility conformance report with test evidence traceable to each criterion?

questions.l1: No Salamanca §7 operational support; inclusion is measured only by placement labels, with no supports/resourcing/training workflows
questions.l3: Tracks some supports and outcomes, but coordination, training workflows, and inclusion outcome monitoring are incomplete
questions.l5: Full Salamanca §7 operationalization with coordinated supports, educator enablement, service delivery tracking, and inclusion outcome dashboards tied to continuous improvement
questions.text: Does the agent support Salamanca Statement §7 implementation by enabling ordinary-school inclusion through (1) individualized supports in mainstream settings, (2) educator training/support workflows, (3) resourcing and service coordination (e.g., speech/OT/AT), and (4) monitoring inclusion outcomes (participation, attainment, wellbeing) rather than placement alone?

questions.l1: Authentication relies on memorised codes or puzzles with no alternative
questions.l3: Password managers and paste are supported, but some steps still require transcription or puzzle solving
questions.l5: Every authentication path passes SC 3.3.8 (paste and password manager support, passkeys or email links, no transcription), verified by automated checks and testing with users with cognitive disabilities
questions.text: Do the agent's sign-in and identity steps meet WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (Minimum), so that no step requires a cognitive function test unless an alternative or assistance mechanism is provided?

questions.l1: The agent ignores assistive technology listed in IEPs
questions.l3: Assistive technology from the IEP is recorded, but compatibility with the agent is not tested
questions.l5: IEP assistive technology needs mapped to tested agent configurations, gaps reported to the IEP team with dates, and compatibility re-tested on each agent release
questions.text: When a learner's IEP requires assistive technology, does the agent ensure the device or service is available and compatible with it, consistent with IDEA regulations at 34 CFR §300.105, and record any gap for the IEP team?

questions.l1: IEP and evaluation data are processed like general data, with no access record
questions.l3: Access is restricted, but there is no §300.614 access record or destruction workflow
questions.l5: Per-access records with party, date and purpose; consent gating before disclosure; documented safeguards; parent notice and destruction workflow with evidence
questions.text: Does the agent handle special-education records under the IDEA Part B confidentiality rules — a record of access naming the party, date and purpose (34 CFR §300.614), parental consent before disclosure (§300.622), safeguards at collection, storage, disclosure and destruction (§300.623), and informing parents when information is no longer needed and destroying it on request (§300.624)?

complianceFrameworks: EU AI Act Art. 5; Annex III point 1(a)/5(a)
digital-citizens-rights.description: Citizen data tied with digital identity and tagged with government identities — supporting tax, travel documents, and rights to private and secure data — AI agents managing digital identity ecosystems, citizen data rights, and public trust infrastructure.
digital-citizens-rights.euAIActClassification: Annex III point 1(a) remote biometric identification (biometric verification that only confirms a claimed identity is excluded) and point 5(a) where identity gates public assistance benefits; Annex III obligations apply from 2 Dec 2027; Art. 5(1)(c), (g), (h) prohibitions apply now
keyRisks: Mass surveillance through digital identity AI integration
Identity fraud amplification through AI-weakened verification
Exclusion of vulnerable populations from digital identity systems
Government data abuse enabled by AI identity correlation
Loss of anonymous participation rights through identity AI requirements
digital-citizens-rights.name: Digital Citizens & Rights

questions.l1: Neither practice is screened: the agent can be configured or invoked to infer sensitive traits from biometric data or to run real-time remote identification in public spaces, and no use-case record shows an Art. 5 assessment
questions.l3: Both practices are prohibited in written policy and screened at use-case intake, but at most one of them is blocked technically at runtime, or exceptions are granted without a recorded prior-authorisation reference
questions.l5: Both practices are blocked at runtime; a real-time identification request is released only with a recorded Art. 5(3) prior-authorisation reference for an Art. 5(1)(h) objective; every block and release is logged, and the log is reviewed by a named owner each release
questions.regulatoryRef: EU AI Act Art. 5(1)(g), 5(1)(h), 5(2)-(3) (apply from 2 Feb 2025); Commission Guidelines on prohibited AI practices (4 Feb 2025, non-binding)
questions.text: Does the agent block the two EU AI Act prohibited biometric practices that identity systems can be repurposed for: biometric categorisation that infers race, political opinions, trade-union membership, religious or philosophical beliefs, sex life or sexual orientation (Art. 5(1)(g)), and use of 'real-time' remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement outside the objectives and prior authorisation set by Art. 5(1)(h) and 5(2)-(3)?

questions.l1: No human rights impact assessment exists for any AI use case that affects citizens
questions.l3: An assessment was done once before deployment with identified risks and mitigations, but it is not repeated on change, mitigations are not tracked to closure, or affected groups were not consulted
questions.l5: Assessment per use case, repeated on each material change and at a set interval, with input from affected groups, mitigations tracked to closure, and grievance cases from an operating channel cited in the next assessment
questions.regulatoryRef: UNGPs Principles 17-21, 29; CoE AI Convention Art. 16
questions.text: Before an AI system that affects citizens' rights goes live, and again on each material change, does the operator carry out a human rights impact assessment that identifies affected groups, assesses the impacts, tracks each mitigation to closure and feeds grievance cases back into the next assessment (UN Guiding Principles 17-21; CoE AI Convention Art. 16 risk and impact management framework)?

questions.l1: Identity-data access, rectification or erasure requests are not routed or answered
questions.l3: Requests are routed and answered, but response times are not measured against the Art. 12(3) period, or refusals are not recorded with a legal basis
questions.l5: Every request is logged with receipt date, identity check, action taken, response date within the Art. 12(3) period and any refusal basis; rectifications propagate to every system the agent reads from, with evidence per request
questions.text: Does the agent route and fulfil citizens' requests to access, rectify and erase government-held digital identity data (GDPR Arts 15-17) within the one-month period of GDPR Art. 12(3), recording any refusal based on a lawful retention duty with its legal basis?

questions.l1: No AI-interaction disclosure on any channel
questions.l3: Disclosure exists only in terms of service or a footer, or only on some channels
questions.l5: Plain-language disclosure at first interaction on every channel, in accessible formats, logged per session, and re-tested on each release
questions.regulatoryRef: EU AI Act Art. 50(1), 50(5); CoE AI Convention Art. 15(2)
questions.text: On every identity-service channel (chat, voice, email, forms), is the agent designed so that people are told they are interacting with an AI system, clearly and distinguishably, at the latest at the first interaction (EU AI Act Art. 50(1) and 50(5), applicable from 2 Aug 2026; CoE AI Convention Art. 15(2))?

questions.l1: No digital inclusion; digital identity systems are inaccessible to persons with disabilities, elderly citizens, and those without digital skills
questions.l3: Agent implements WCAG 2.1 AA for digital identity interfaces, but does not provide alternative access channels or implement full CRPD Art. 9 accessibility requirements
questions.l5: Full digital inclusion with WCAG 2.1 AA+ implementation, CRPD Art. 9 multi-channel access (digital and non-digital), assisted identity enrollment for vulnerable populations, digital literacy support, and universal design per EU Accessibility Directive
questions.regulatoryRef: CRPD Art. 9; EU Web Accessibility Directive 2016/2102
questions.text: Does the agent implement digital inclusion safeguards per UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD) Article 9 accessibility and EU Web Accessibility Directive for digital identity services?

questions.l1: High-risk identity transactions accept single-factor or SMS-only authentication and no assurance-level mapping exists
questions.l3: Multi-factor authentication is used, but the mapping from transaction type to assurance level is missing or incomplete, or the authenticators used do not meet the mapped level
questions.l5: A documented mapping assigns every transaction type an assurance level under each applicable scheme; authenticators meet the mapped level's requirements; each authentication event records the level achieved; the mapping is reviewed when NIST, ISO or eIDAS implementing acts change
questions.regulatoryRef: eIDAS 2.0 Art. 8 (assurance levels); NIST SP 800-63B-4 (July 2025, supersedes SP 800-63B); ISO/IEC 29115:2013
questions.text: Does the agent authenticate citizens for identity services at an assurance level matched to each transaction's risk, using a documented mapping to eIDAS assurance levels (low, substantial, high) in EU flows, NIST SP 800-63B-4 authenticator assurance levels in US federal flows, and ISO/IEC 29115:2013 levels of assurance, and does it apply the authenticator requirements of the mapped level, including the highest level where the mapping requires it?

questions.l1: No identity breach response; identity system incidents are handled without GDPR Art. 33 notification timelines or NIS2 significant incident escalation procedures
questions.l3: Agent detects identity system anomalies and can initiate breach notification, but does not automate GDPR Art. 33 72-hour notification or NIS2 Art. 23 competent authority reporting
questions.l5: Full identity incident response with automated GDPR Art. 33 notification within 72 hours, NIS2 Art. 23 significant incident reporting, affected identity holder notification per Art. 34, credential revocation workflows, and forensic-ready audit evidence preservation
questions.text: Does the agent implement breach notification and identity compromise response per GDPR Article 33 72-hour notification and EU NIS2 Directive Article 23 for identity infrastructure incidents?

questions.l1: No social-scoring screen: the agent can build or apply behaviour-based scores to identity holders
questions.l3: Social scoring is prohibited in policy and use cases are screened at intake, but no runtime check stops a scoring request or a score from being used across contexts
questions.l5: Use-case intake records a guideline-based Art. 5(1)(c) assessment; runtime rules block cross-context use of behaviour scores; blocked requests are logged and reviewed each release
questions.regulatoryRef: EU AI Act Art. 5(1)(c) (applies from 2 Feb 2025); Commission Guidelines on prohibited AI practices (4 Feb 2025, non-binding)
questions.text: Does the agent refuse to evaluate or classify people over time based on their social behaviour or known, inferred or predicted personal characteristics where the resulting score leads to detrimental treatment in unrelated contexts or treatment disproportionate to the behaviour (EU AI Act Art. 5(1)(c) social scoring), including when it is asked to rank identity holders for access to public services?

questions.l1: No Art. 5a wallet control: wallet assurance level high is not defined, evidenced, or auditably enforced
questions.l3: Some wallet features exist (e.g., selective disclosure), but assurance level high governance and evidence are incomplete or non-auditable
questions.l5: Full Art. 5a EUDI Wallet implementation with assurance level high governance, relying-party verification, cross-border acceptance, and auditor-ready evidence packs for issuance/authentication/attestation lifecycles
questions.regulatoryRef: eIDAS 2.0 Art. 5a (EUDI Wallet), assurance level high
questions.text: Does the agent implement eIDAS 2.0 Article 5a EU Digital Identity Wallet requirements with explicit support for wallet assurance level high, including (1) assurance claim governance, (2) evidence bundles for high assurance (issuance + authentication + attribute attestation), (3) relying-party verification flows, (4) cross-border acceptance checks, and (5) auditable wallet lifecycle controls (issuance, suspension, revocation, recovery)?

questions.l1: Use cases are not classified against Annex III, or a high-risk use case has none of the Art. 9-14 artefacts
questions.l3: Each use case is classified with a rationale, and some artefacts exist (e.g. logs, documentation), but risk-management or data-governance evidence is missing
questions.l5: Classification per use case with rationale (including any reliance on the Annex III 1(a) verification exclusion); the complete Art. 9-14 artefact set is versioned with each agent release; open gaps are tracked against 2 Dec 2027
questions.regulatoryRef: EU AI Act Annex III point 1(a), point 5(a); EU AI Act Art. 9-12, 14; EU AI Act Art. 113 as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (Annex III high-risk obligations from 2 Dec 2027)
questions.text: Where the agent is, or is part of, a high-risk AI system under EU AI Act Annex III in this pack's scope — remote biometric identification (point 1(a); biometric verification that only confirms a claimed identity is excluded) or eligibility for essential public assistance benefits (point 5(a)) — does it hold the Chapter III Section 2 evidence set (risk management Art. 9, data governance Art. 10, technical documentation Art. 11, record-keeping Art. 12, human oversight Art. 14), with a gap plan dated against 2 Dec 2027, when those obligations apply to Annex III systems?

questions.l1: No explicit-consent controls: special-category attributes are processed/shared without explicit consent evidence or withdrawal handling
questions.l3: Consent is captured, but is not granular/purpose-scoped or lacks auditable receipts and withdrawal enforcement
questions.l5: Full Art. 9(2)(a) explicit-consent governance with granular consent receipts, withdrawal enforcement, and audit-ready logs tied to attribute disclosure events
questions.text: When special-category attributes are stored or shared via the digital identity wallet, does the agent implement GDPR Art. 9(2)(a) explicit consent with (1) purpose-scoped consent prompts, (2) granular attribute-level consent, (3) withdrawal/refresh rules, (4) consent receipt + audit logs, and (5) safeguards against coerced consent in public-service contexts?

questions.l1: Affected persons cannot obtain any explanation of the AI system's role
questions.l3: Explanations are given on request, but they are generic and not specific to the decision
questions.l5: Decision-specific explanations generated from logged inputs and outputs, delivered in plain language within a set time, and tracked through to any appeal
questions.text: When a decision based on the output of an Annex III high-risk AI system produces legal effects for a person, can the affected person obtain a clear and meaningful explanation of the AI system's role and the main elements of the decision, as EU AI Act Article 86 provides?

questions.l1: No route to contest AI-influenced identity decisions
questions.l3: A contest route exists, but the person is not told the AI's role or the information relied on, or contested cases are not reviewed by a human
questions.l5: Each adverse decision notice states the AI's role and the main information relied on; contests are reviewed by a named human within a published time limit; outcomes are logged; the notice names the complaint route to the market surveillance authority
questions.regulatoryRef: CoE AI Convention Art. 14, Art. 15; EU AI Act Art. 85
questions.text: When an AI-influenced decision affects a person's identity status or rights, does the operator give the person the information needed to contest it, a route to contest it before a human, and the procedural safeguards the CoE AI Convention requires (Art. 14 remedies, Art. 15 procedural safeguards), and does it signpost the complaint route to the market surveillance authority (EU AI Act Art. 85)?

questions.l1: The wallet is the only access route and the agent requests whole credentials rather than selected attributes
questions.l3: Selective disclosure is used, but agent-initiated exchanges do not appear on the dashboard, or no equivalent non-wallet route exists
questions.l5: Only attributes needed for the stated purpose are requested; each agent-initiated exchange produces a dashboard entry; erasure requests from the dashboard are honoured with evidence; an equivalent non-wallet route is available and tested
questions.text: In EU Digital Identity Wallet flows the agent initiates or mediates, does it preserve the user controls of eIDAS Art. 5a: selective disclosure of attributes (Art. 5a(4)), an entry on the wallet's transaction dashboard for each exchange so the user can review it and request erasure (Art. 5a(4)), and no disadvantage for people who do not use a wallet (Art. 5a(15))?

questions.l1: The agent requests broad attribute sets and caches presentation payloads
questions.l3: Requests are limited to registered attributes, but transaction content is retained in agent logs or the relying party is not identified to the user
questions.l5: A registration-bound attribute allow-list is enforced at runtime; the relying party is shown to the user; logs hold metadata only; a periodic check produces evidence that no transaction content is stored
questions.text: When the agent acts for a relying party that requests data from an EU Digital Identity Wallet, does it act only as or under a registered relying party, request only the attributes registered for the stated use, identify the relying party to the user, and avoid storing data about the content of the transaction, as eIDAS Art. 5b requires of relying parties and intermediaries?

digital-health-record.certificationPath: L1 Basic EHR data capture → L2 HL7 FHIR interoperability → L3 Full HIPAA/GDPR compliant data governance → L4 Cross-border health data exchange per EHDS → L5 Autonomous longitudinal health record governance with patient-sovereign data control
digital-health-record.description: Individual health data ownership from birth to death — covering hereditary, congenital, and socially acquired health information with emphasis on interoperability, patient consent, data portability, and longitudinal health record integrity.
digital-health-record.euAIActClassification: Art. 6(1) and Annex I (Regulation (EU) 2017/745 MDR, 2017/746 IVDR) where the agent is, or is a safety component of, a medical device; Annex III §5(a) where public authorities use it to evaluate eligibility for healthcare services
keyRisks: PHI breach through AI-mediated data aggregation across systems
Health record integrity compromise from automated data reconciliation errors
Genetic discrimination from AI-accessible hereditary health data
Patient consent violation through automated data sharing without granular authorization
Interoperability failures causing clinical decision errors from incomplete records
digital-health-record.name: Digital Health Record

questions.l1: The agent uses a shared or human account for EHR access; its actions cannot be attributed to it
questions.l3: The agent has its own identity and authenticates on its main EHR path, but some paths (batch jobs, tool connectors) use shared credentials, or emergency access is not defined
questions.l5: Every EHR access path the agent uses carries a unique agent identity plus the identity of the person it acts for; authentication (MFA where offered) is enforced and evidenced in configuration; emergency access is time-bound and reviewed after use; access logs are exportable on request
questions.text: Does the agent operate under its own unique user identity (HIPAA §164.312(a)(2)(i)) and authenticate itself and every person or entity it acts for (§164.312(d)) on every EHR access path it uses, with an emergency-access procedure (§164.312(a)(2)(ii))?

questions.l1: Requests are delayed, throttled or refused (including automated requests) with no recorded exception
questions.l3: Most requests are fulfilled and some limitations cite an exception, but exception records are incomplete or automated requests are handled differently without a recorded reason
questions.l5: Every limitation of an EHI request has a record naming the Part 171 exception and its conditions; request-to-fulfilment times are measured; automated and human requests follow the same policy; the proposed HTI-5 change is tracked as proposed
questions.regulatoryRef: 21st Century Cures Act §4004; 42 U.S.C. 300jj-52; 45 CFR Part 171
questions.text: Does the agent avoid information blocking (21st Century Cures Act §4004; 42 U.S.C. 300jj-52; 45 CFR Part 171) by fulfilling requests to access, exchange or use EHI, including requests made by automated or agentic clients, without unnecessary delay, and by recording the specific Part 171 exception relied on whenever it limits a request?

questions.l1: No provenance tracking; health record modifications are not systematically attributed or timestamped
questions.l3: Provenance is written for creates and some updates, but agent identity or source entities are missing on part of the records
questions.l5: Sampled agent-written records all have Provenance with agent identity, accountable person, timestamp and source entities; provenance gaps are detected by an automated check and reported
questions.text: Does the agent write an HL7 FHIR R4 Provenance resource for every health-record create, update or delete it performs, naming itself as Provenance.agent and the records it read as Provenance.entity?

questions.l1: No digital consent management; patient consent is paper-based with no granular data sharing controls
questions.l3: Agent manages FHIR Consent resources with basic permit/deny policies, but does not support granular purpose-of-use consent or dynamic consent modification by patients
questions.l5: Patient-sovereign consent management with granular purpose-of-use controls, dynamic consent modification, consent propagation across federated systems, automated consent enforcement at data access point, and transparent consent audit trail per GDPR Art. 7(1)
questions.regulatoryRef: HL7 FHIR R4 Consent Resource; GDPR Art. 9(2)(a)
questions.text: Does the agent support patient consent management per FHIR Consent resource and GDPR Article 9(2)(a) explicit consent for health data processing?

questions.l1: PHI is stored or transmitted unencrypted with no documented risk decision
questions.l3: Main stores and APIs are encrypted, but some paths (model endpoints, logs, caches, partner interfaces) are not, or exceptions are undocumented
questions.l5: Encryption at rest and in transit is evidenced by configuration for every store and interface the agent uses, including model endpoints and logs; each exception has a documented risk analysis and compensating control; a key-management procedure exists
questions.text: Does the agent encrypt the PHI it stores and transmits, including prompts, retrieved context, tool payloads and logs, per HIPAA §164.312(a)(2)(iv) and §164.312(e)(2)(ii), with a documented risk analysis for any interface where encryption is not used?

questions.l1: No cross-border data exchange capability; health records are siloed within national systems
questions.l3: Agent exchanges patient summaries cross-border in a pilot or national format, but secondary-use processing has no data-permit check
questions.l5: Primary-use exchange uses the European exchange format through the national contact point; every secondary-use processing job is linked to a data permit and runs only in the permitted environment; application dates are tracked per Art. 105
questions.text: Does the agent support cross-border primary-use exchange via MyHealth@EU (Regulation (EU) 2025/327 Art. 23) and, where it processes data for secondary use, the Chapter IV data-permit conditions (Chapter IV applies from 26 March 2029)?

questions.l1: No genetic data protections; hereditary health information is accessible without additional safeguards beyond general PHI controls
questions.l3: Agent classifies genetic data separately and applies enhanced access controls, but does not prevent indirect genetic inference from non-genetic health data or manage genetic counseling consent
questions.l5: Comprehensive genetic data governance with enhanced classification, inference prevention controls, genetic counseling consent tracking, research use consent management per GINA §102, and automated genetic discrimination risk assessment for data sharing requests
questions.text: Does the agent prevent genetic discrimination per Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act (GINA) Title I §101 and GDPR Article 9(1) genetic data protections?

questions.l1: No ISO 27799 alignment; health information security controls are ad hoc without systematic implementation
questions.l3: Access control and cryptographic controls are implemented for the agent, but the rest of the applicable control set has no statement of applicability
questions.l5: A statement of applicability covers the agent, its model endpoints and tools; each applicable control has implementation evidence; the set is reviewed at least yearly
questions.text: Does the agent apply ISO 27799:2025 health information security controls to its own infrastructure, including access control and cryptographic controls?

questions.l1: No IHE profile implementation; document sharing is proprietary with no standardized metadata
questions.l3: Agent registers and queries documents via XDS.b (incl. ITI-18 Registry Stored Query) with required metadata, but XCA cross-community query is not supported or not tested
questions.l5: XDS.b (incl. ITI-18) and XCA transactions pass interoperability testing (test report on file); metadata validation errors are logged and resolved; error handling for stored queries is tested
questions.regulatoryRef: IHE ITI TF-3 §4.2 — XDS.b; IHE XCA Profile
questions.text: Does the agent support IHE XDS.b document sharing with metadata per IHE ITI TF-3 §4.2 and cross-community access per XCA profile?

questions.l1: No completeness check against USCDI data classes
questions.l3: Completeness is checked for some data classes, or against USCDI v1 (expired 2026-01-01)
questions.l5: Every produced or exchanged record is checked against USCDI v3 data classes; missing elements are reported with source system; completeness rates are tracked over time
questions.text: Does the agent check the completeness of the records it produces or exchanges against the USCDI v3 data classes adopted at 45 CFR 170.213, and report missing required elements?

questions.l1: No minimum necessary enforcement; users can access full patient records regardless of their role or purpose
questions.l3: Agent implements role-based access that limits PHI exposure by job function, but does not dynamically adjust access based on specific transaction purpose or clinical context
questions.l5: Dynamic minimum necessary enforcement with purpose-of-use based access filtering, clinical context awareness, automated de-identification for non-treatment uses per §164.514(a), and granular field-level access logging
questions.text: Does the agent enforce minimum necessary standard per HIPAA §164.502(b) and §164.514(d) for all PHI disclosures and internal access?

questions.l1: Classification is asserted without analysis (for example every health use labelled Annex III 5(a)), or not recorded
questions.l3: Classification is documented per intended purpose, but registration scope or the amended application dates (2 Dec 2027 Annex III; 2 Aug 2028 Annex I) are not recorded
questions.l5: A classification record per intended purpose states the legal path and reasoning; Art. 49 registration exists before market placement where Annex III applies; application dates match Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 and are re-checked when amending acts are published
questions.regulatoryRef: EU AI Act Art. 6; EU AI Act Art. 49; Regulation (EU) 2026/1744
questions.text: Does the agent's provider record, per intended purpose, whether the EHR AI function is high-risk via Art. 6(1) and Annex I Section A points 11-12 (MDR/IVDR device AI) or via Art. 6(2) and Annex III point 5(a), (c) or (d), register it under EU AI Act Art. 49 only where Annex III applies, and record the application date for each path as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744?

questions.l1: Audit logs are incomplete, user-editable, or not time-stamped; record changes cannot be reliably reconstructed
questions.l3: Maintains audit logs and timestamps for key events, but tamper resistance, retention controls, and linkage to record lifecycle events are incomplete
questions.l5: For sampled FDA-regulated records, the audit trail shows who/what (agent or person), when, and the prior value for every change; users cannot edit the trail; trails are retained as long as the records and are exportable for inspection
questions.text: For records required under FDA regulations that the agent creates, modifies or deletes, does it keep secure, computer-generated, time-stamped audit trails that record operator entries and actions without obscuring prior values (21 CFR §11.10(e))?

questions.l1: No clinical evaluation governance; clinical evidence is not tracked and changes do not trigger evaluation updates
questions.l3: Maintains a clinical evaluation plan and some evidence linkage, but updates are manual and post-market data is not systematically incorporated
questions.l5: Continuous clinical evaluation lifecycle with evidence graph linkage to features/claims, change-triggered evaluation updates, post-market surveillance signal ingestion, and audit-ready clinical evaluation reporting per Art. 61
questions.text: If the system (or modules) are MDR-relevant software, does the agent support EU MDR 2017/745 Article 61 clinical evaluation governance (clinical evidence linkage, evaluation plan, update triggers, and post-market data incorporation)?

questions.l1: FHIR endpoints are partial/non-conformant; no published capability statement or conformance testing; integrations are brittle
questions.l3: Publishes capability statement and supports common interactions, but conformance testing is incomplete and edge cases cause interoperability failures
questions.l5: CapabilityStatement is published and versioned; automated conformance tests cover every declared interaction and run on each release; exchange failures are logged and tracked to resolution
questions.text: Does the agent publish an HL7 FHIR R4 CapabilityStatement for its FHIR endpoints and pass conformance tests for the interactions it declares?

questions.l1: Agent API and bulk-export access is not logged or is logged under a shared identity
questions.l3: Access is logged with agent identity, but purpose, scope or the represented user is missing for bulk exports
questions.l5: Every API and bulk-export access is logged with agent identity, user, purpose and scope; logs are reviewed on a schedule; anomalies are investigated with records
questions.text: Does the agent log every access it makes through the standardized FHIR API (45 CFR §170.315(g)(10)), including bulk exports, with its own identity, the user it acts for, purpose and scope, as HIPAA audit controls (45 CFR §164.312(b)) require for systems containing ePHI?

questions.l1: No source attributes for AI interventions; clinicians cannot see intended use, development data or validation
questions.l3: Source attributes are maintained for some predictive DSIs but are not versioned with model updates, and risk management evidence is ad hoc
questions.l5: Versioned source attributes for every predictive DSI, risk management evidence (validity, fairness, safety, security) linked to each release, and a tracked regulatory-status flag for the HTI-5 proposal
questions.text: For predictive decision support interventions surfaced through certified health IT, does the agent populate the source attributes required by 45 CFR §170.315(b)(11)(iv) and support intervention risk management under (b)(11)(vi), tracking the HTI-5 proposal (90 FR 60970) to remove these requirements?

questions.l1: Agent access is logged under a shared service identity and is not available to patients
questions.l3: Agent access is attributed and retained, but patients cannot obtain it, or restrictions are enforced manually
questions.l5: Each access records provider or person, date and time, and data accessed; it is available to the patient for at least three years; Art. 8 restrictions are enforced by the system and tested; application dates per Art. 105 (2029-03-26 for priority categories) tracked
questions.text: Does the agent make every access it makes to personal electronic health data attributable, so that natural persons can obtain information on each access for at least three years (Regulation (EU) 2025/327 Art. 9), and does it honour access restrictions under Art. 8 without revealing them to providers?

questions.l1: Part 2 records are handled like other PHI; no consent check
questions.l3: Part 2 records are tagged, but consent scope is not checked per disclosure or the §2.32 notice is missing
questions.l5: Every disclosure of tagged Part 2 records is gated on a matching consent and carries the §2.32 notice; segmentation is tested; disclosures are logged and auditable
questions.text: When the agent summarises, routes or discloses substance use disorder records from a 42 CFR Part 2 program, does it check Part 2 consent (§2.31), attach the required notice and copy of consent to each disclosure (§2.32), and keep these records segregated from general HIPAA handling, as required since the 2026-02-16 compliance date?
