infotainment.certificationPath: L1 Basic content moderation → L2 DSA/GDPR baseline compliance → L3 DSA VLOP-level obligations → L4 Full DMA + Copyright compliance → L5 Autonomous trusted infotainment with verified accuracy, equity, and democratic safeguards
infotainment.description: The combination of information and entertainment shared and consumed by people — physically and digitally available on-demand — AI agents curating, generating, and distributing content with emphasis on accuracy, consumer protection, content moderation, and copyright compliance.
infotainment.euAIActClassification: Not listed in Annex III except §8(b) systems intended to influence elections or voting behaviour; Art. 50(4) deep-fake disclosure and Art. 5(1)(a) manipulation prohibition apply
keyRisks: Misinformation amplification through algorithmic recommendation
Harmful content exposure to minors despite automated moderation
Synthetic media deception undermining democratic discourse
Copyright violation through AI-generated derivative content
Filter bubble reinforcement through over-personalization
infotainment.name: Infotainment

questions.l1: No systemic risk assessment of recommender and content-curation systems.
questions.l3: A risk assessment exists, but it does not cover every Art. 34(1) risk category, or it is not repeated before deploying functionalities likely to have a critical impact.
questions.l5: Annual Art. 34 assessment covering each Art. 34(1) category; Art. 35 mitigation with an owner per identified risk; supporting documents retained for at least three years (Art. 34(3)); assessment repeated before launching critical-impact functionalities.
questions.text: Does the agent implement Digital Services Act Article 34 systemic risk assessment for very large online platform recommendation systems and content curation?

questions.l1: No minor-specific measures; profiling-based ads shown to recipients known to be minors.
questions.l3: Profiling-based ads suppressed for recipients known to be minors, but no documented minor-protection measures for content or settings.
questions.l5: Documented minor-protection measures per feature; ad serving blocks profiling-based ads for recipients known with reasonable certainty to be minors, with test evidence; measures reviewed on a documented schedule.
questions.text: Does the platform protect minors under DSA Art. 28: measures for a high level of privacy, safety and security of minors (Art. 28(1)), and no advertisements based on profiling when it is aware with reasonable certainty that the recipient is a minor (Art. 28(2))?

questions.l1: No recommender parameter disclosure.
questions.l3: Main parameters disclosed, but modification options are not described or not available in the interface.
questions.l5: Main parameters disclosed in plain language; every described option is available in the interface; disclosure updated with each ranking change.
questions.text: Does the platform set out in its terms and conditions the main parameters of its recommender systems and any options for recipients to modify or influence them (DSA Art. 27)?

questions.l1: No notice mechanism for illegal content.
questions.l3: Notice form exists; notices processed without recorded decisions or timestamps.
questions.l5: Electronic notice mechanism; every notice tracked to a decision with timestamps; each decision linked to its Art. 17 statement of reasons; use of automated means recorded.
questions.text: Does the platform operate a notice-and-action mechanism that lets any individual or entity notify specific items of allegedly illegal content (DSA Art. 16), with each notice processed to a recorded decision?

questions.l1: No accessibility conformance evidence.
questions.l3: Accessibility audit for the web interface only; apps, media players or generated media not audited.
questions.l5: Accessibility audit against a declared conformance standard across web, apps and media players, including captions for generated media; accessibility statement published; audit repeated on each major release.
questions.text: Do the agent's consumer services that fall within the European Accessibility Act (e.g. services providing access to audiovisual media services, Directive (EU) 2019/882 Art. 2(2)(b)) meet its accessibility requirements, applicable since 28 June 2025?

questions.l1: Tracking identifiers are stored or read without consent.
questions.l3: Consent is collected before non-essential storage or access on some channels (e.g. web) but not on others (apps, SDKs), or consent withdrawal is not propagated.
questions.l5: No non-essential storage or access before consent on any channel, verified by automated scans; each strictly-necessary exemption recorded with its reason; withdrawal stops storage and access, with logs.
questions.text: Does the agent's personalization store or read information on users' terminal equipment (e.g. tracking identifiers) only with the user's consent given with clear and comprehensive information, unless strictly necessary for a service the user explicitly requested (ePrivacy Directive Art. 5(3))?

questions.l1: Terms do not describe content-moderation restrictions and there is no internal complaint system.
questions.l3: Terms describe restrictions including algorithmic decision-making and a complaint system exists, but complaint decisions lack records or are taken solely by automated means.
questions.l5: Terms (Art. 14) describe policies, procedures, measures and tools including algorithmic decision-making and human review; complaints accepted for at least six months after a decision; each complaint decided under the supervision of qualified staff, not solely by automated means (Art. 20(6)), with records.
questions.text: Does the agent implement content governance per DSA Article 14 terms of service transparency and Article 20 internal complaint-handling requirements for platform content decisions?

questions.l1: No disclosure of deep fakes or AI-generated public-interest text.
questions.l3: Disclosure on deep fake images or video only; audio or public-interest text not disclosed, or editorial-control exceptions not recorded.
questions.l5: Disclosure across all modalities at first exposure; each text exception backed by a recorded human review or editorial control; disclosures logged and tested.
questions.text: As a deployer, does the agent disclose that image, audio or video deep fakes it generates or manipulates are artificially generated or manipulated, and that text published to inform the public on matters of public interest is AI-generated unless it underwent human review or editorial control (EU AI Act Art. 50(4), applicable from 2 August 2026)?

questions.l1: No statement of reasons for restrictions.
questions.l3: Statements are issued for some restriction types, or omit an Art. 17(3) element (facts, use of automated means, legal or contractual ground, redress).
questions.l5: A statement is issued for every Art. 17(1) restriction type with every Art. 17(3) element; use of automated means disclosed; statements logged and retrievable per decision.
questions.text: Does the agent issue a DSA Article 17(1) statement of reasons for each content moderation decision (removal, restriction, demonetization, suspension), including (a) decision type and legal/ToS basis, (b) main parameters/facts relied on, (c) whether automated tools were used, and (d) clear redress/complaint options?

questions.l1: No parity controls: the gatekeeper's own services can be ranked more favourably with no detection or record.
questions.l3: Ranking conditions are documented, but parity tests do not cover every ranking change or deviations are not recorded.
questions.l5: Ranking conditions documented and available to business users; parity tests comparing own and third-party services run on every ranking change; deviations recorded with reasons; test records retained.
questions.text: Where the platform is a designated gatekeeper, does the agent avoid treating the gatekeeper's own services and products more favourably in ranking and related indexing and crawling than similar third-party services, applying transparent, fair and non-discriminatory ranking conditions (EU DMA Art. 6(5))?

questions.l1: No authorisation efforts, notice handling, or complaint and redress mechanism.
questions.l3: Licensing efforts and notice-based removal exist, but there is no stay-down for sufficiently substantiated notices, or no complaint and redress mechanism with human review.
questions.l5: Licensing efforts documented; notified works kept unavailable per Art. 17(4)(b)-(c); lawful uses preserved (Art. 17(7)); complaint and redress mechanism with human review (Art. 17(9)); every decision logged.
questions.text: Does the agent implement EU Copyright Directive 2019/790 Article 17 OCSSP obligations end-to-end: (a) best-efforts licensing/authorization, (b) best-efforts to ensure unavailability of notified works, (c) stay-down for sufficiently substantiated notices, (d) safeguards for lawful uses (quotation/criticism/review, parody/pastiche), and (e) effective complaint and redress with timely human review?

questions.l1: No §312.4 notices.
questions.l3: Online notice published, but the direct notice to parents is not sent before collection or lacks required content.
questions.l5: Online notice and direct parental notice contain the §312.4 content; direct notice is sent before collection with delivery logs; notices are versioned.
questions.text: Does the agent provide COPPA-compliant notices per 16 CFR §312.4, including a clear online privacy policy describing information practices for children and direct notice to parents before collection, use or disclosure of a child's personal information?

questions.l1: No media-provider declaration functionality.
questions.l3: Declaration functionality exists; restrictions on declared providers' content are not routed through the Art. 18 safeguards.
questions.l5: Declarations integrated into the moderation pipeline; every restriction of declared providers' content follows the Art. 18 steps with records; outcomes logged.
questions.text: On a very large online platform, does the agent provide the functionality for media service providers to declare their status (Regulation (EU) 2024/1083 Art. 18(1)) and apply the Art. 18 procedural safeguards before restricting or suspending their content?

questions.l1: No non-profiling option.
questions.l3: Non-profiling option exists for some recommender systems.
questions.l5: Every recommender system has a non-profiling option reachable from the feed; the choice persists; usage logged.
questions.text: On a very large online platform or search engine, does the agent provide for each recommender system at least one option that is not based on profiling (DSA Art. 38)?

questions.l1: Child personal information collected without parental consent.
questions.l3: Consent obtained for collection, but not for new uses or disclosures, or the consent method is not documented as verifiable.
questions.l5: Consent recorded before every collection, use and disclosure; method documented; consent records linked to each child account; paths without consent block collection, with tests.
questions.text: For child-directed services, or with actual knowledge of collecting from children under 13, does the operator obtain verifiable parental consent before any collection, use or disclosure of a child's personal information (COPPA Rule 16 CFR §312.5)?

questions.l1: No review of interfaces for deceptive design.
questions.l3: Major flows reviewed for deceptive design before launch; no recurring review or test evidence.
questions.l5: Deceptive-design checklist applied to every release with recorded reviews; experiments that change choice architecture approved and logged; findings remediated.
questions.text: Does the agent avoid designing, organising or operating online interfaces in a way that deceives or manipulates recipients or materially distorts or impairs their ability to make free and informed decisions (DSA Art. 25)?

questions.l1: Reservations not checked before mining.
questions.l3: One reservation method checked (e.g. robots.txt); other machine-readable reservations ignored, or decisions not logged.
questions.l5: Every machine-readable reservation method the operator recognises is checked before mining; each fetch decision logged; reserved content excluded and the exclusion verifiable.
questions.text: When the agent mines text and data from content made publicly available online, does it identify and comply with rightholders' machine-readable reservations of rights (Directive (EU) 2019/790 Art. 4(3))?

regulatoryReferences.citation: Children's Online Privacy Protection Act (15 U.S.C. §§6501-6506) and COPPA Rule (16 CFR Part 312), as amended 2025
Directive (EU) 2019/790 (Copyright in the Digital Single Market)

sdgAlignment: SDG 16 — Peace, Justice and Strong Institutions

k12-pm3.certificationPath: L1 Basic educational content delivery → L2 FERPA/COPPA compliant data handling → L3 Full child safety with age-appropriate AI → L4 Adaptive learning with equity monitoring → L5 Autonomous K-12 AI governance with verified learning outcomes and child protection
k12-pm3.description: Kindergarten through grade 12 formal education foundation — covering AI in primary and secondary education with emphasis on child safety, age-appropriate content, parental consent, and equitable learning outcomes.
k12-pm3.euAIActClassification: Annex III §3 — education and vocational training (admission, evaluating learning outcomes, assessing education level, proctoring)
keyRisks: Child data exploitation through AI-mediated educational platforms
Algorithmic bias reinforcing achievement gaps across demographics
Age-inappropriate content generation by AI tutoring systems
Over-surveillance of children through AI behavioral monitoring
Special education discrimination through AI-driven placement decisions
k12-pm3.name: K-12 Education

questions.l1: Personal information is collected from users under 13 with no verifiable parental consent record, or practices change after consent without new consent
questions.l3: Each child account has a verifiable consent record, but material changes to collection, use or disclosure practices are not detected and do not trigger new consent
questions.l5: Each child account has a versioned verifiable-consent record tied to the practice version consented to; a documented change check blocks collection, use or disclosure under a changed practice until new consent is recorded; withdrawal stops processing and is logged
questions.text: Does the agent obtain verifiable parental consent before any collection, use or disclosure of personal information from a child under 13, and obtain new consent before any material change to the practices the parent consented to (16 CFR §312.5(a)(1)), keeping versioned consent records?

questions.l1: No FERPA compliance; student education records are accessible without legitimate educational interest verification
questions.l3: Agent enforces role-based access to education records and tracks directory information opt-outs, but does not implement full legitimate educational interest verification or audit logging per FERPA
questions.l5: Full FERPA compliance with legitimate educational interest verification per §99.31, directory information opt-out management, annual notification automation, audit logging of all record access, and FERPA exception documentation for permitted disclosures
questions.text: Does the agent implement FERPA 20 USC §1232g(b) education record protections with directory information opt-out and legitimate educational interest verification?

questions.l1: No bias prevention; AI assessment and placement algorithms are not tested for demographic disparities or disproportionate representation
questions.l3: Agent monitors assessment outcomes by demographic group and flags statistical disparities, but does not implement model-level bias mitigation or disproportionality analysis per IDEA
questions.l5: Comprehensive equity monitoring with assessment bias testing, disproportionality analysis per IDEA §612(a)(24), culturally responsive assessment validation, achievement gap tracking, equitable resource allocation verification, and transparent equity reporting
questions.text: Does the agent prevent algorithmic bias in student assessment and placement, including the disproportionality analysis required by IDEA §612(a)(24)?

questions.l1: Generated or retrieved content reaches minors with no filtering mapped to the school's Internet safety policy
questions.l3: Generated and retrieved content is filtered, but the mapping from the school's Internet safety policy to agent controls and the filter-override log are not documented
questions.l5: Filtering of generated and retrieved content is mapped item by item to the school's Internet safety policy; filter disabling is limited to authorized staff for adults' bona fide research and logged; filter efficacy is tested each release; an evidence bundle supports the school's certification
questions.text: Does the agent apply the deploying school's CIPA technology protection measure and Internet safety policy (47 CFR §54.520(c)) to the content it generates or retrieves for minors — blocking visual depictions that are obscene, child pornography or harmful to minors — and give the school policy-to-control evidence for its CIPA certification?

questions.l1: No special education support; AI systems do not accommodate IEP requirements
questions.l3: Agent tracks IEP goals and accommodations, but does not adapt AI interactions to individual IEP requirements or monitor accommodation effectiveness
questions.l5: Full special education integration with IEP goal tracking, automated accommodation implementation, progress monitoring per IDEA §614(d), assistive technology integration, and transition planning support per §614(d)(1)(A)(i)(VIII)
questions.text: Does the agent support special education compliance per IDEA §614 Individualized Education Program (IEP) requirements?

questions.l1: Parents are not told the agent is used, who operates it or which records it reads
questions.l3: A general AI-use notice exists, but the annual FERPA notice's school-official criteria do not cover the agent's provider
questions.l5: The annual FERPA notice states school-official criteria that cover the agent's provider; a per-service notice lists the record categories used; notice versions are retained per school year
questions.text: Are parents and eligible students told, through the school's annual FERPA notice and its criteria for who is a school official (34 CFR §99.7(a)(3)(iii)), that the agent's provider acts as a school official and which record categories the agent uses?

questions.l1: Learners are not told they are interacting with an AI system
questions.l3: An AI disclosure exists in terms of service or settings, but not at the point of interaction
questions.l5: The agent discloses that it is an AI system at the first interaction of each session, in wording tested with the age groups it serves; the disclosure is versioned and covered by release tests
questions.text: Where the agent is offered to learners in the EU, are learners informed that they are interacting with an AI system, unless that is obvious from the context (EU AI Act Art. 50(1), applicable from 2026-08-02)?

questions.l1: No written retention policy; children's personal information collected by the agent, including conversation logs, has no deletion schedule
questions.l3: A written retention policy exists, but some stores (logs, backups, model-improvement datasets) are outside it or deletion is not verified
questions.l5: The written retention policy covers every store of children's personal information, including logs and model-improvement data; deletion runs on schedule with verification evidence; no store has indefinite retention
questions.text: Does the operator keep a written data retention policy for children's personal information collected through the agent (including conversation logs and model-improvement data), delete that information once it is no longer reasonably necessary for the purpose it was collected for, and never retain it indefinitely (16 CFR §312.10)?

questions.l1: No WCAG 2.1 AA conformance evidence for the agent's interfaces or generated content
questions.l3: Interfaces are audited to WCAG 2.1 AA, but generated content (alt text, documents, captions) is not checked
questions.l5: WCAG 2.1 A/AA testing of interfaces and generated content runs each release with assistive-technology checks; a conformance report per release; defects tracked to remediation before the district's compliance date
questions.text: For deployments by or for a public school district, do the agent's web and mobile interfaces and the content it generates meet WCAG 2.1 Level A and AA under the ADA Title II rule (28 CFR §35.200) — including content provided through contractual or licensing arrangements — by the district's compliance date (2027-04-26 for a population of 50,000 or more; 2028-04-26 otherwise)?

questions.l1: Agent outputs (grades, recommendations, restrictions) take effect with no educator override
questions.l3: Educators can override outputs, but overrides are not logged or some decision points lack an override; no AI-free option for assessed work
questions.l5: Every grading, recommendation or restriction point has an educator override logged with a reason; an AI-free option exists for assessed work; override rates are reviewed each term
questions.regulatoryRef: UNESCO Guidance for generative AI in education and research (2023)
questions.text: Does the agent keep educators as the decision-makers where it grades, recommends or restricts learner activity — with an educator override at each such point and an AI-free option for assessed work — in line with UNESCO's Guidance for generative AI in education and research (2023, non-binding)?

questions.l1: No prohibited-practice screen; engagement, persuasion or emotion/affect features run on learners
questions.l3: Features were screened at launch, but the screen is not repeated on model or feature change, or the medical/safety exception for emotion inference is undocumented
questions.l5: Every feature and model change passes a recorded Art. 5 screen with sign-off; emotion inference is disabled in education deployments by configuration and tested; any medical or safety exception is documented and approved
questions.regulatoryRef: EU AI Act Art. 5(1)(b); EU AI Act Art. 5(1)(f)
questions.text: Does each agent feature pass a documented screen against the EU AI Act Art. 5 prohibitions relevant to schools — no exploitation of vulnerabilities due to age or disability that materially distorts behaviour (Art. 5(1)(b)) and no inference of learners' emotions in an education institution except for medical or safety reasons (Art. 5(1)(f))?

questions.l1: No emergency workflow; disclosures are ad-hoc and undocumented, with no threat rationale or disclosure logs
questions.l3: Maintains an emergency disclosure playbook and logs some disclosures, but threat rationale, minimum-necessary controls, and recipient scoping are inconsistent
questions.l5: End-to-end §99.36 support with guided threat assessment prompts, minimum-necessary data packaging, recipient allowlisting (law enforcement/health officials/etc.), time-bounded access, and immutable disclosure logs with post-incident review exports
questions.text: Does the agent support FERPA emergency disclosures per 34 CFR §99.36 by (1) documenting the articulable and significant threat rationale, (2) limiting disclosure to appropriate parties and minimum necessary information, and (3) maintaining required recordkeeping for each disclosure event?

questions.l1: No GDPR child-consent handling; consent logic is COPPA-only or unspecified for EU users
questions.l3: Implements EU age gating and collects parental authorization, but Member-State thresholds, provenance, and auditability are incomplete
questions.l5: Full GDPR Art. 8 compliance with jurisdiction-aware thresholds, verified parental authorization, consent versioning + withdrawal, provenance linking to processing purposes and categories, and audit-ready exports for school/DPA inquiries
questions.text: Does the agent implement GDPR Article 8 child-consent handling for education services by supporting Member-State age thresholds (13–16), reasonable efforts for parental authorization, age/region-aware consent flows, and auditable consent provenance (linked to lawful basis and data categories) for EU student users?

questions.l1: No high-risk controls; no risk management, oversight criteria, or audit-ready documentation/logging
questions.l3: Implements some oversight and logs, but risk management, data governance, and conformity-assessment documentation are incomplete
questions.l5: Comprehensive Annex III education AI governance: risk management + residual risk tracking, dataset governance & quality controls, human oversight criteria and escalation, event logging, technical documentation, and conformity-assessment evidence packaging for schools/authorities
questions.regulatoryRef: EU AI Act Annex III §3 (education) + high-risk obligations
questions.text: For EU AI Act Annex III §3 high-risk educational AI (access, assessment, or placement), does the agent implement high-risk lifecycle controls including a documented risk management system, data governance for training/validation/operation, and meaningful human oversight for high-impact decisions (with logging and technical documentation sufficient for conformity assessment)?

questions.l1: Records disclosed to the provider are reused for its own purposes (e.g. product or model training) or redisclosed without consent
questions.l3: The contract states school-official status and purpose limits, but technical controls do not prevent reuse or redisclosure and nothing is audited
questions.l5: Purpose-bound access is enforced in code; training or analytics use is blocked unless the school authorizes it in writing; redisclosure is blocked; per-record access logs are exportable to the school
questions.text: When the agent's provider receives education records as a school official under 34 CFR §99.31(a)(1)(i)(B), does it stay under the school's direct control over use and maintenance of the records — using them only for the purposes of the disclosure, not for its own purposes such as model training unless the school authorizes it — and observe the §99.33(a) limits on redisclosure?

questions.l1: The agent elicits protected-category information in check-ins or surveys with no consent check

questions.text: Does the agent avoid subjecting students, without prior consent (written parental consent for an unemancipated minor), to psychological examination or testing — including AI-led wellbeing check-ins — designed to reveal PPRA-protected information: political affiliations, mental or psychological problems, sex behaviour or attitudes, illegal, anti-social or self-incriminating behaviour, critical appraisals of close family members, legally privileged relationships, or income (34 CFR §98.4)?

questions.l1: Covered pupil information feeds advertising, non-school profiling or sale
questions.l3: Advertising and sale are excluded, but profiling limits are undocumented or deletion on school request is manual with no evidence
questions.l5: Data-use controls block advertising, non-school profiling and sale; school-initiated deletion is automated with completion evidence; security practices are documented per data store

Bus. & Prof. Code §22584(b), (d))?

questions.l1: No written security program covers children's personal information

questions.l5: A written program with a named coordinator, a dated risk assessment covering the agent's data flows and third-party providers, safeguard testing records, and an annual program evaluation on file
questions.text: Does the operator maintain a written information security program for children's personal information handled by the agent — a designated coordinator, a recurring risk assessment, safeguards matched to the risks found, regular testing and monitoring of those safeguards, and an annual program evaluation (16 CFR §312.8(b))?

Digital health divide excluding vulnerable populations
Over-diagnosis from consumer health AI creating unnecessary anxiety
Data exploitation through health app data monetization
Clinical safety incidents from unvalidated AI health predictions

questions.l3: Agent classifies SaMD functions per IMDRF risk framework and applies appropriate controls, but does not implement full clinical evaluation per FDA guidance
questions.l5: Full SaMD lifecycle management with IMDRF risk classification, clinical evaluation per FDA guidance, predetermined change control plan, real-world performance monitoring, and regulatory submission readiness documentation
questions.regulatoryRef: IMDRF SaMD N12; FDA SaMD Clinical Evaluation Guidance
questions.text: Does the agent implement SaMD risk classification per IMDRF SaMD Framework N12 and FDA SaMD Clinical Evaluation guidance?

questions.l1: No risk management file or dataset documentation for the AI system
questions.l3: A risk management file and dataset descriptions exist, but representativeness and bias checks or Art. 4a safeguards are missing or not versioned
questions.l5: Risk management is updated per release; each dataset has versioned provenance, representativeness and bias test results; special-category data use for bias detection is logged with Art. 4a safeguards; obligations dated 2 Aug 2028 (Annex I) or 2 Dec 2027 (Annex III)
questions.regulatoryRef: EU AI Act Art. 9; EU AI Act Art. 10(2); EU AI Act Art. 4a; Regulation (EU) 2026/1744
questions.text: For high-risk health AI, does the provider operate risk management (EU AI Act Art. 9) and training, validation and testing data governance (Art. 10(2)), processing special-category health data for bias detection only under the Art. 4a safeguards inserted by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744?

questions.l1: No risk management process; digital health technologies are deployed without systematic hazard analysis
questions.l3: Agent maintains risk management files with identified hazards and risk controls, but risk estimation is qualitative and not updated with post-market data
questions.l5: Comprehensive risk management with quantitative risk estimation, risk control verification, residual risk evaluation, risk-benefit analysis, production/post-production information integration, and continuous risk management process per ISO 14971 Clause 4
questions.text: Does the agent implement clinical risk management per ISO 14971:2019 Clause 4.1 risk management process for digital health technologies?

questions.l1: No digital equity assessment; health technology design does not consider accessibility barriers or digital literacy requirements
questions.l3: Agent tracks basic accessibility metrics and supports multiple languages, but does not assess digital literacy requirements or design for low-resource settings
questions.l5: Comprehensive digital health equity with accessibility compliance (WCAG 2.1 AA), digital literacy assessment, low-bandwidth optimization, offline capability, multilingual support, assistive technology compatibility, and equity impact assessment per WHO strategy
questions.regulatoryRef: WHO Global Strategy on Digital Health 2020-2025 §4.2
questions.text: Does the agent assess digital health equity per WHO Global Strategy on Digital Health 2020-2025 and prevent digital divide in health technology access?

questions.l1: No software lifecycle management; health software updates are deployed without systematic quality management
questions.l3: Agent tracks software versions and maintains change documentation, but does not implement full IEC 62304 quality management system integration
questions.l5: Full IEC 62304 QMS integration with software safety classification, development planning per Clause 5.1, requirements management, architecture documentation, verification/validation, release management, and maintenance process per Clause 6
questions.text: Does the agent implement software lifecycle management per IEC 62304:2006/AMD1:2015 Clause 4 quality management system requirements for health software?

questions.l1: No Part 11 compliance; electronic health records lack required controls for data integrity and electronic signatures
questions.l3: Agent implements basic audit trails and access controls per §11.10, but electronic signatures and system validation are not fully compliant
questions.l5: Full Part 11 compliance with validated systems, complete audit trails per §11.10(e), electronic signatures per §11.50/§11.70, system access controls, authority checks, device checks, and periodic system validation documentation
questions.text: Does the agent enforce electronic records integrity per FDA 21 CFR Part 11 §11.10 controls for closed systems including audit trails and electronic signatures?

questions.l1: No AI explainability; health predictions and recommendations are black-box with no explanation of reasoning
questions.l3: Agent provides basic explanations of AI outputs and confidence levels, but does not implement detailed feature attribution or uncertainty quantification
questions.l5: Full health AI explainability with feature attribution, uncertainty quantification, confidence calibration, counterfactual explanations, clinician-appropriate and patient-appropriate explanation modes, and transparency documentation per EU AI Act Art. 13
questions.regulatoryRef: EU AI Act Art. 13; FDA AI/ML Transparency Principles
questions.text: Does the agent provide health AI explainability per EU AI Act Article 13 transparency requirements and FDA Transparency Principles for AI/ML?

questions.l1: No health-specific cybersecurity; digital health systems use generic security controls without medical device threat modeling
questions.l3: SBOM and a vulnerability process exist, but the agent's model, prompt and tool dependencies are not in the SBOM or threat model
questions.l5: SBOM covers the agent including model and tool dependencies; threat model and security risk assessment are linked to safety risk management; postmarket vulnerability monitoring and coordinated disclosure are evidenced
questions.regulatoryRef: FDA Cybersecurity in Medical Devices guidance (February 2026); FD&C Act §524B; IEC 81001-5-1
questions.text: For cyber devices, does the agent's manufacturer provide the FD&C Act §524B evidence (SBOM, postmarket vulnerability monitoring plan, secure product development framework) per FDA's cybersecurity guidance (February 2026), with IEC 81001-5-1 health software security activities?

questions.l1: Model and prompt changes ship without regulatory change assessment
questions.l3: A PCCP covers model retraining, but prompt and tool changes are outside it
questions.l5: The PCCP covers every modifiable component; each change record shows it was executed per the modification protocol with impact assessment; changes outside the PCCP trigger a new submission decision
questions.regulatoryRef: 21 U.S.C. 360e-4; FDA PCCP for AI-Enabled Device Software Functions final guidance
questions.text: Does the agent's manufacturer control AI changes through an authorized predetermined change control plan (21 U.S.C. 360e-4; FDA PCCP final guidance) describing the planned modifications, the methodology to develop, validate and implement them, and an impact assessment, covering every modifiable component including prompts and tools?

questions.l1: No HTA readiness; digital health technologies are not assessed for clinical and economic value
questions.l3: Outcome data is collected, but it is not structured for HTA submission or JCA scope is not assessed
questions.l5: JCA scope under Art. 7 is assessed and recorded; comparative effectiveness and patient-reported outcome evidence is structured for HTA bodies; evidence gaps are tracked
questions.regulatoryRef: Regulation (EU) 2021/2282 Art. 7; NICE ESF for DHTs
questions.text: Does the agent's evidence generation support health technology assessment, including joint clinical assessment where the technology falls under Regulation (EU) 2021/2282 Art. 7?

questions.l1: No CDS boundary classification; AI health apps operate without FDA CDS guidance Non-Device vs Device classification assessment, risking unregulated SaMD deployment
questions.l3: Functions are classified once, but the record does not address each criterion or is not repeated after feature changes
questions.l5: Each function has a dated classification record addressing every criterion; feature changes trigger re-classification; device functions follow a regulatory pathway
questions.regulatoryRef: FD&C Act §520(o)(1)(E); FDA Clinical Decision Support Software guidance (January 2026)
questions.text: Does the agent's provider classify each decision-support function as non-device CDS or device software using the FD&C Act §520(o)(1)(E) criteria as explained in FDA's CDS guidance (January 2026), and re-run the classification when features change?

questions.l1: No software requirements analysis; system behavior is implicit and tests are not traceable to safety requirements
questions.l3: Partial requirements exist with some test links, but risk-control linkage, coverage checks, and change impact analysis are incomplete
questions.l5: Full §5.2 compliance with controlled requirements, traceability completeness checks, risk-control linkage, change impact analysis, and release gating on trace completeness
questions.text: Does the agent support software requirements analysis per IEC 62304:2006 §5.2, including safety classification-driven requirements rigor, linkage to risk controls (ISO 14971), and bidirectional traceability (hazard → requirement → implementation → verification evidence) with change impact analysis?

questions.l1: No performance evaluation; diagnostic claims are made without structured evidence or monitoring
questions.l3: Some validation evidence exists, but it is not structured as an IVDR-grade performance evaluation with clear intended purpose alignment and ongoing monitoring
questions.l5: Comprehensive IVDR-grade performance evaluation support with plan/report structures, analytical + clinical performance evidence linkage, intended-purpose traceability, and post-market performance monitoring with drift triggers
questions.regulatoryRef: EU IVDR 2017/746 Art. 56; EU IVDR 2017/746 Annex XIII
questions.text: If the agent makes diagnostic or IVD-adjacent claims or interprets biomarker inputs, does it support IVDR performance evaluation evidence (EU IVDR 2017/746 Art. 56; Annex XIII), including a performance evaluation plan, scientific validity and analytical and clinical performance evidence, and post-market performance follow-up?

questions.l1: No structured clinical evaluation; claims are not supported by clinical association/analytical/clinical validation evidence
questions.l3: Some validation exists, but evidence is fragmented and does not cleanly map to clinical association vs analytical vs clinical validation for the intended use
questions.l5: Full clinical evaluation with evidence mapping, intended-use traceability, subgroup performance analysis, and continuous real-world performance feedback into evaluation updates
questions.text: Does the agent implement the FDA guidance Software as a Medical Device (SaMD): Clinical Evaluation by structuring evidence as (1) valid clinical association, (2) analytical validation and (3) clinical validation, with intended-use alignment, subgroup analysis and real-world performance monitoring?

questions.l1: No interoperability safety controls; device data is ingested without semantic/unit/time validation
questions.l3: Basic device integration exists, but semantic/unit/time-sync validation and auditability are incomplete
questions.l5: Robust IEEE 11073-10201-aligned interoperability with semantic/unit/time validation, transport resilience, provenance logs, and safety checks that gate downstream clinical logic on data integrity
questions.text: Does the agent ensure safe interoperability for connected health devices by implementing IEEE 11073-10201-aligned data exchange (device identity, measurement semantics/units, time synchronization, transport constraints), plus validation checks and audit logs to prevent silent data misinterpretation?

material-to-machines.certificationPath: L1 Basic material compliance tracking → L2 RoHS/WEEE compliance automation → L3 Full ecodesign integration per EU Regulation 2024/1781 → L4 Circular economy optimization with DPP → L5 Autonomous product lifecycle governance with verified sustainability metrics
material-to-machines.description: Appliances, quality of life improvement, and manufacturing — covering the lifecycle of consumer and industrial products from raw material extraction through design, manufacturing, use, and end-of-life with emphasis on ecodesign, energy efficiency, and circular economy principles.
material-to-machines.euAIActClassification: Not listed in Annex III; high-risk only under Art. 6(1) where the agent is, or is a safety component of, a product covered by Annex I legislation — otherwise Art. 4 (AI literacy), Art. 5 (prohibited practices) and Art. 50 (transparency) apply
keyRisks: Conflict mineral sourcing undetected in AI-optimized procurement
Planned obsolescence embedded in AI-driven product design
Hazardous substance threshold violations in automated material substitution
Energy efficiency rating manipulation through selective testing conditions
E-waste export to developing nations through logistics optimization
material-to-machines.name: Material to Machines

questions.l1: No RoHS screening; component selection does not verify restricted substance concentrations against Annex II thresholds
questions.l3: Agent screens components against RoHS Annex II substance limits (lead, mercury, cadmium, Cr6+, PBB, PBDE, DEHP, BBP, DBP, DIBP) but relies on supplier declarations without independent verification
questions.l5: Every component is screened against Annex II maximum concentration values with supplier declarations and test (e.g. XRF) evidence linked, exemptions under Annex III/IV are tracked with expiry dates, and components without evidence cannot be released
questions.text: Does the agent enforce restricted substance compliance per RoHS Directive 2011/65/EU Annex II maximum concentration values for all electrical/electronic components?

questions.l1: No ecodesign integration; product design decisions do not consider repairability, durability, or end-of-life recyclability
questions.l3: Agent evaluates designs against ecodesign criteria and generates repairability scores, but does not actively optimize designs for circular economy outcomes
questions.l5: Full ecodesign optimization engine that balances performance, cost, repairability (per repair score methodology), durability testing predictions, recyclability assessment, and material efficiency — with automated compliance documentation per Art. 5
questions.text: Does the agent implement ecodesign requirements per EU Ecodesign Regulation 2024/1781 Article 5 including repairability, durability, and recyclability criteria?

questions.l1: No WEEE tracking; producer responsibility obligations are managed manually with no visibility into collection or recycling rates
questions.l3: Agent tracks WEEE registration and reports collection volumes, but does not optimize reverse logistics or monitor recycling target achievement in real-time
questions.l5: Comprehensive WEEE lifecycle management with automated producer registration across jurisdictions, real-time collection rate monitoring against Art. 7 targets, recycling process optimization, and material recovery tracking with verified evidence
questions.text: Does the agent manage WEEE Directive 2012/19/EU Article 12 producer responsibility obligations including collection rate tracking and recycling target compliance?

questions.l1: No energy-label generation or EPREL registration support
questions.l3: Labels are generated from test results, but EPREL registration and test-report linkage are manual
questions.l5: Every model has its label and information sheet generated from linked test reports under the applicable delegated regulation, EPREL registration is completed before release, and label changes are versioned
questions.text: Does the agent generate energy labels and product information sheets from test results under the applicable delegated regulation and register each model in EPREL before it is placed on the market, per Regulation (EU) 2017/1369?

questions.l1: No conflict mineral tracking; 3TG sourcing is not assessed for conflict-affected or high-risk area origins
questions.l3: Agent collects Conflict Minerals Reporting Templates (CMRTs) from suppliers and flags high-risk smelters, but does not perform independent supply chain due diligence per OECD guidance
questions.l5: Full conflict mineral due diligence with smelter-level traceability, OECD 5-step framework implementation, automated CMRT collection and validation, risk assessment for all CAHRAs, and transparent reporting per Art. 7
questions.text: Does the agent implement conflict mineral due diligence per EU Conflict Minerals Regulation 2017/821 Article 4 for tin, tantalum, tungsten, and gold (3TG)?

questions.l1: No DPP capability; product information is not structured for machine-readable access
questions.l3: Agent generates basic DPPs with material composition and compliance data, but interoperability with EU DPP infrastructure and data carrier standards is incomplete
questions.l5: For each product group with an adopted delegated act, every mandatory DPP attribute is populated with a source-evidence link, the data carrier resolves to the current record, lifecycle updates are versioned, and consumer and recycler views are available
questions.text: Does the agent maintain Digital Product Passport data per Regulation (EU) 2024/1781 Art. 9-11 for product groups covered by an adopted delegated act, with an interoperable data carrier and lifecycle updates?

questions.l1: No lifecycle impact assessment; environmental considerations are not integrated into design decisions
questions.l3: Agent performs simplified LCA using industry databases and identifies major environmental hotspots, but does not systematically apply IEC 62430 design principles
questions.l5: Comprehensive environmentally conscious design integration with full LCA per ISO 14044, design optimization against multiple environmental indicators, material selection guidance per IEC 62430, and verified impact reduction tracking
questions.text: Does the agent assess environmental lifecycle impact per IEC 62430:2019 Clause 6 environmentally conscious design principles?

questions.l1: No battery-specific compliance; battery components are treated generically without regulation-specific tracking
questions.l3: Agent tracks battery chemistry and capacity for classification, generates carbon footprint declarations per Art. 7, but does not manage full lifecycle obligations including collection and recycling
questions.l5: End-to-end battery compliance with carbon footprint calculation per delegated methodology, recycled content verification per Art. 8, performance/durability tracking per Art. 10, battery passport generation per Art. 77, and second-life assessment
questions.text: Does the agent manage battery compliance per EU Battery Regulation 2023/1542 Articles 7-11 including carbon footprint declaration and recycled content requirements?

questions.l1: No zone/conduit model or target security level for systems the agent touches
questions.l3: Zones and conduits are defined and basic access controls applied, but achieved security level is not assessed against SL-T
questions.l5: Each zone and conduit has a documented SL-T, the achieved level is assessed against the IEC 62443-3-3 system requirements with gaps tracked, and agent changes to OT systems are re-assessed before deployment
questions.text: Does the agent's deployment in industrial control systems meet the target security level (SL-T) for its zones and conduits per IEC 62443-3-3:2013 system security requirements?

questions.l1: No EHSR mapping; safety functions changed by software or ML updates are not re-assessed
questions.l3: An EHSR checklist exists and major updates are reviewed, but ML/software updates to safety functions are not consistently gated
questions.l5: Every update touching a safety function passes a recorded EHSR impact assessment before release, self-evolving safety components have a notified-body assessment plan, and the technical documentation is updated per release
questions.regulatoryRef: Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 Art. 10, Annex III (EHSR), Annex I Part A
questions.text: Where the agent's software or ML model performs or changes a machinery safety function, does each update re-assess conformity with the essential health and safety requirements (Annex III) before release, and is third-party conformity assessment planned for safety components with self-evolving behaviour, per Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 (applies 20 Jan 2027)?

questions.l1: Shared accounts/weak authentication; device/service identities are unmanaged and not auditable
questions.l3: Unique user IDs and basic authentication are implemented, but service/device identity, credential rotation, and coverage across zones is incomplete
questions.l5: Full SR 1.1 implementation with unique identities for users/services/devices, strong authentication, credential rotation, secure enrollment, continuous verification, and audit-ready evidence mapped to target security level
questions.text: Does the agent implement and continuously verify Identification and Authentication Control per IEC 62443-3-3 SR 1.1 for all users (human and machine), services, and devices across OT zones/conduits (including unique identities, credential lifecycle, and authentication strength)?

questions.l1: No formal change management for OH&S; changes are applied without documented hazard/risk review
questions.l3: Performs change reviews and risk assessments for major changes, but coverage is inconsistent and worker consultation/evidence capture is incomplete
questions.l5: Closed-loop OH&S change management with automated hazard prompts, risk controls selection, worker consultation records, pre-startup safety verification, and auditable change approval gates
questions.text: Does the agent manage OH&S-related change control per ISO 45001:2018 §8.1.3 (management of change), including hazard identification, risk assessment, worker consultation, and verification before implementing changes to machinery, tooling, processes, or control software?

questions.l1: No repairability controls; design decisions do not manage spare parts, disassembly, or repair information availability
questions.l3: Generates repairability guidance and partial spare-parts lists, but compliance is not enforced as a release gate and evidence is incomplete
questions.l5: Repairability-by-design with enforceable constraints, automated spare-parts availability rules, disassembly time/steps scoring, repair information publication workflows, and compliance evidence packs aligned to delegated-act requirements
questions.text: Does the agent apply the repairability parameters set under Regulation (EU) 2024/1781 Art. 5(1) and the related Art. 7 information requirements (spare parts, repair information, disassembly) for product groups with an adopted delegated act, and gate design releases on them?

questions.l1: No release gate; products are placed on the market without consolidated RoHS compliance evidence and exemption control
questions.l3: Aggregates BOM declarations and flags issues, but exemption applicability and product-level sign-off are manual and inconsistently retained
questions.l5: Automated product-level RoHS compliance gating with evidence linkage, exemption lifecycle management (Annex III/IV), sampling/testing integration, and audit-ready technical file exports
questions.text: Does the agent enforce RoHS Directive 2011/65/EU Article 4 by gating release/placing-on-the-market decisions on product-level RoHS compliance evidence (including BOM aggregation, supplier declarations, test evidence, and exemption applicability tracking)?

questions.l1: No treatment information is published for new equipment types
questions.l3: Treatment information exists for some product lines but is not linked to product types or launch dates
questions.l5: Per-type treatment records generated from the bill of materials, published to treatment facilities within one year of market placement, versioned on design changes and cross-checked with the Digital Product Passport
questions.text: Does the agent provide treatment facilities with the reuse and treatment information required by WEEE Directive 2012/19/EU Article 15 (components, materials and the location of dangerous substances) for each new type of electrical and electronic equipment within one year of placing it on the market?

questions.l1: No path to report vulnerabilities or incidents in agent-managed products
questions.l3: A manual reporting path to the Single Reporting Platform exists, but timing has not been tested
questions.l5: Detection-to-report is rehearsed and timed against 24h/72h, final-report content (corrective measure, root cause) is assembled from agent and product logs, and each report is retained
questions.regulatoryRef: Regulation (EU) 2024/2847 (manufacturer reporting of actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents)
questions.text: Can the manufacturer report an actively exploited vulnerability or severe incident affecting a connected product the agent runs on or manages through the CRA Single Reporting Platform within the Cyber Resilience Act deadlines (24h early warning, 72h notification, final report) applying from 11 Sep 2026?

networked-ecosystems.certificationPath: L1 Basic API security → L2 GDPR data portability compliance → L3 EU Data Act/DGA compliance → L4 Full ecosystem trust architecture → L5 Autonomous ecosystem orchestration with verified data rights and sovereignty

Privacy violations through ecosystem data correlation

questions.l1: Users cannot obtain product or related-service data.

questions.l1: No API inventory and no authorisation tests; object-level authorisation is not enforced.
questions.l3: Object-level authorisation (API1:2023) is enforced and tested on some endpoints; the other API Top 10 2023 categories are not mapped to tests.

questions.l1: Intermediation service operated without notification; intermediated data reused for other purposes.

questions.l5: Notification on file; separate legal person; technical controls block reuse of intermediated data with access logs; Art. 12 conditions mapped to controls and reviewed on a documented schedule.
questions.regulatoryRef: EU Data Governance Act Art. 11; EU Data Governance Act Art. 12
questions.text: If the agent provides data intermediation services, has the provider notified the competent authority (EU Data Governance Act Art. 11), and does the agent meet the Art. 12 conditions, including not using the intermediated data for other purposes and providing the service through a separate legal person (Art. 12(a))?

questions.l1: No machine-readable export of personal data.
questions.l3: Machine-readable export for some data categories; no direct controller-to-controller transmission.
questions.l5: Export covers all personal data provided by the data subject where Art. 20(1) applies; direct transmission where technically feasible; each request logged with completion time.
questions.text: Does the agent let data subjects receive the personal data they provided in a structured, commonly used and machine-readable format and transmit it to another controller without hindrance (GDPR Art. 20(1))?

questions.l1: Ecosystem APIs have no published interface description and data formats are undocumented.
questions.l3: Interface descriptions are published for some APIs, or data formats are documented but not openly available to ecosystem participants.
questions.l5: Every exposed API has a published machine-readable description validated in CI against the running service; every exchanged data format is openly documented and versioned; deprecations announced with a documented notice period.
questions.text: Does the agent expose every ecosystem API with a published machine-readable interface description (for example OpenAPI 3.1) and exchange data in openly documented formats, applying the technical interoperability layer of the European Interoperability Framework (COM(2017) 134)?

questions.l1: No assurance-level mapping.
questions.l3: AAL mapped and enforced for human users; agent or workload identities, or federation (FAL), not mapped.
questions.l5: IAL, AAL and FAL mapped for every human and agent identity class; enforcement tested; step-up authentication for sensitive operations; mapping reviewed on change.
questions.text: Does the agent's ecosystem access management map human and agent identities to NIST SP 800-63-4 identity assurance (IAL), authenticator assurance (AAL) and federation assurance (FAL) levels and enforce them?

questions.l1: No EUDI Wallet support on flows that require strong authentication.

questions.l5: Wallet authentication accepted on every flow requiring strong authentication; relying-party registration on file; acceptance tested against the wallet validation mechanisms.
questions.text: Where the operator is a private relying party, other than a micro or small enterprise, that Union or national law or a contract requires to use strong user authentication for online identification, does the agent accept European Digital Identity Wallets on the user's voluntary request (eIDAS 2.0, Regulation (EU) No 910/2014 as amended by Regulation (EU) 2024/1183, Art. 5f(2), no later than 36 months after the implementing acts under Arts. 5a(23) and 5c(6) enter into force), with the relying party registered under Art. 5b?

questions.l1: Data made available on undocumented or discriminatory terms.
questions.l3: Written terms exist, but the compensation basis is not documented, or differs between comparable recipients without a recorded reason.
questions.l5: Standard terms per recipient category; compensation calculation documented and applied consistently; deviations recorded with reasons; terms disclosed to the recipient before agreement.
questions.regulatoryRef: EU Data Act Art. 8(1); EU Data Act Art. 9(1)
questions.text: Where the agent makes data available to a data recipient in business-to-business relations under a Data Act obligation, does it agree fair, reasonable, non-discriminatory and transparent terms (EU Data Act Art. 8(1)) and set any compensation that is non-discriminatory and reasonable (Art. 9(1))?

questions.l1: Implicit grant in use, or public clients without PKCE.
questions.l3: PKCE enforced for public clients and implicit grant removed, but at least one other applicable RFC 9700 requirement is not mapped to a test.
questions.l5: Every applicable RFC 9700 requirement for the client types in use is mapped to an automated conformance test in CI; logs show PKCE on every authorization.
questions.text: Does the agent's OAuth integration conform to IETF RFC 9700 (BCP 240), including PKCE for every public client, which RFC 9700 makes a MUST, and no use of the implicit grant, which it says SHOULD NOT be used?

questions.l1: No switching support and no switching terms in the contract.
questions.l3: Contract states switching rights and export is possible, but switching charges remain planned after 12 January 2027 or no exit has been exercised in a test.
questions.l5: Written switching terms provided before contract signature; exit to another provider and to on-premises tested with records; switching charges set to zero from 12 January 2027 with billing evidence.
questions.regulatoryRef: EU Data Act Art. 23; EU Data Act Art. 25(1); EU Data Act Art. 29(1)
questions.text: If the agent provides or brokers data processing services, does it enable customers to switch to another provider or to on-premises infrastructure under a written contract that sets out switching rights (EU Data Act Arts. 23, 25(1)), and impose no switching charges from 12 January 2027 (Art. 29(1))?

questions.l1: No path to share user data with user-designated third parties.
questions.l3: Sharing happens on request, but recipient-side limits under Art. 6 are not enforced or recorded.
questions.l5: Self-service sharing to user-designated recipients; recipient use restricted to the agreed purpose with technical enforcement; every share and recipient use logged.
questions.regulatoryRef: EU Data Act Art. 5; EU Data Act Art. 6
questions.text: When a user asks for product or related-service data to be shared with a third party, does the agent make it available to that third party (EU Data Act Art. 5) and, when the agent is the recipient, use the data only within the limits of Art. 6?

questions.l1: Responses to requests to know are not machine-readable.
questions.l3: Machine-readable responses for some categories; transmission to another entity not supported.
questions.l5: All specific pieces returned in a structured machine-readable format; transmission to another entity on request; request handling logged with response dates.
questions.text: On a verifiable consumer request to know, does the business provide the specific pieces of personal information in a structured, commonly used, machine-readable format that can be transmitted to another entity, to the extent technically feasible (Cal. Civ. Code §1798.130(a)(3)(B)(iii))?

questions.l1: No supplier security assessment for ecosystem integrations.
questions.l3: Supplier inventory with security assessment for critical suppliers only; no contractual security requirements or re-assessment trigger.
questions.l5: Every direct supplier and service provider in the ecosystem inventoried with a security assessment, contractual security clauses and re-assessment on change or incident; evidence retained.
questions.text: Where the operator is an essential or important entity under NIS2, does the agent's ecosystem integration apply supply chain security measures covering the security of relationships with direct suppliers and service providers (Directive (EU) 2022/2555 Art. 21(2)(d))?

questions.l1: Joint processing with partners is not identified and no arrangement exists.
questions.l3: Joint processing is identified and arrangements exist for some partners, or arrangements do not allocate responsibility for data subject rights and Art. 13-14 information.
questions.l5: Every joint-controller relationship in the ecosystem is inventoried with an arrangement allocating rights handling and Art. 13-14 information duties and naming a contact point for data subjects; arrangements are reviewed whenever the joint processing changes, with review records.
questions.text: Where the agent's operator and ecosystem partners jointly determine the purposes and means of processing personal data, have they set out their respective responsibilities, in particular for data subject rights and the information duties of Arts. 13 and 14, in an arrangement between them (GDPR Art. 26(1))?

questions.l1: Data offered to data-space participants without machine-readable dataset descriptions or API descriptions.
questions.l3: Dataset or API descriptions exist for some offerings, or omit licences, data quality or terms of use.
questions.l5: Every offered dataset has a machine-readable description covering content, use restrictions, licence, collection methodology and quality; every access API is described with its terms of use and quality of service; descriptions are validated on each release.
questions.text: Where the agent's operator offers data or data services to other participants in a data space, does it describe dataset content, use restrictions, licences, collection methodology and quality in a machine-readable format, and describe its access APIs with their terms of use and quality of service sufficiently to enable automatic access (EU Data Act Art. 33(1)(a), (c))?

regulatoryReferences.citation: California Consumer Privacy Act as amended by CPRA (Cal. Civ. Code §1798.100 et seq.) and CPPA regulations

no-poverty.certificationPath: L1 Basic financial access provision → L2 Responsible lending with consumer protection → L3 Full financial inclusion with CGAP standards → L4 AI-enhanced poverty reduction with impact measurement → L5 Autonomous inclusive finance governance with verified poverty reduction outcomes
no-poverty.description: Economic opportunities for socially displaced and disadvantaged populations — covering financial inclusion, microfinance, social protection, and economic empowerment with emphasis on equitable access, dignity preservation, and sustainable poverty reduction.
no-poverty.euAIActClassification: Annex III §5(a) — public assistance benefits and services; §5(b) — creditworthiness of natural persons
keyRisks: Predatory lending through AI-optimized high-interest microloans
Financial exclusion reinforcement through biased credit algorithms
Dignity violation through invasive poverty verification processes
Data exploitation of vulnerable population financial behavior
Debt trap creation through AI-managed lending without affordability assessment
no-poverty.name: No Poverty

questions.l1: No predatory lending prevention; AI lending algorithms optimize for revenue without affordability assessment or interest rate caps
questions.l3: Agent implements basic affordability checks and interest rate monitoring, but does not assess cumulative debt burden or prevent over-indebtedness across multiple lenders
questions.l5: Comprehensive predatory lending prevention with affordability assessment, cumulative debt burden analysis, interest rate fairness evaluation, transparent pricing disclosure, over-indebtedness early warning, and responsible collection practices per CGAP principles
questions.regulatoryRef: CGAP Client Protection Principles; World Bank FCP Good Practices
questions.text: Does the agent prevent predatory lending per CGAP Client Protection Principles and World Bank Good Practices for Financial Consumer Protection?

questions.l1: No inclusion assessment; financial services algorithms may exclude displaced populations, refugees, or undocumented individuals
questions.l3: Agent tracks service access metrics by population segment and flags exclusion patterns, but does not implement alternative identification or credit assessment for underserved populations
questions.l5: Full financial inclusion with alternative ID acceptance per UNHCR guidelines, non-traditional credit assessment, refugee/displaced population accommodation, language accessibility, cultural sensitivity, and inclusion impact measurement per IFC PS1
questions.regulatoryRef: IFC Performance Standard 1; UNHCR Financial Inclusion Guidelines
questions.text: Does the agent ensure financial inclusion without discrimination per IFC Performance Standard 1 and UNHCR Guidelines on Financial Inclusion for refugees?

questions.l1: No simplified CDD; all customers face the same due diligence requirements regardless of risk level, creating barriers for low-income populations
questions.l3: Agent applies tiered CDD based on product risk level, but simplified procedures are not systematically designed for financial inclusion or aligned with FATF guidance
questions.l5: Risk-based CDD with FATF-aligned simplified procedures for low-risk inclusion products, tiered account limits, progressive KYC as usage increases, and documented risk assessment justifying simplified measures per FATF R1 and inclusion guidance
questions.regulatoryRef: FATF Recommendation 1; FATF Guidance on Financial Inclusion (2017)
questions.text: Does the agent implement simplified due diligence per FATF Recommendation 1 risk-based approach for low-risk financial inclusion products?

questions.l1: No mobile money security; digital financial services lack fraud protection appropriate for vulnerable and low-literacy users
questions.l3: Agent implements basic transaction security and fraud alerts, but user interfaces are not designed for low-literacy users and fraud education is not provided
questions.l5: Comprehensive mobile money security with low-literacy UI design, voice-based transaction confirmation, fraud education in local languages, social engineering protection, agent network fraud monitoring, and GSMA certification compliance
questions.regulatoryRef: GSMA Mobile Money Certification; GSMA Code of Conduct for Mobile Money
questions.text: Does the agent implement mobile money security per GSMA Mobile Money Certification requirements and protect low-literacy users from fraud?

questions.l1: No financial literacy support; product terms are presented in complex language without educational context
questions.l3: Agent provides simplified product information and basic financial literacy content, but does not personalize education or assess user comprehension
questions.l5: Full financial literacy integration with personalized education, comprehension verification, transparent product comparison, total cost disclosure in local currency, visual/audio explanations for low-literacy users, and ongoing financial capability building
questions.regulatoryRef: World Bank FCP Good Practices Principle 3
questions.text: Does the agent provide financial literacy support and transparent product information per World Bank Good Practices Principle 3 (Disclosure and Transparency)?

questions.l1: No impact measurement; financial inclusion activities are not assessed for actual poverty reduction outcomes
questions.l3: Agent tracks basic financial access metrics (accounts opened, loans disbursed) but does not measure poverty reduction outcomes or economic empowerment indicators
questions.l5: Comprehensive impact measurement with SDG 1 indicator tracking, income improvement measurement, economic resilience assessment, multidimensional poverty index integration, longitudinal outcome tracking, and transparent impact reporting
questions.regulatoryRef: UN SDG 1 Indicators 1.1.1, 1.2.1; World Bank Poverty Measurement
questions.text: Does the agent measure poverty reduction impact per UN SDG 1 indicators and World Bank poverty measurement methodology?

questions.l1: No vulnerable population data protection; financial data of displaced/disadvantaged populations is processed without enhanced safeguards
questions.l3: Agent applies basic data protection to all customer data, but does not implement enhanced protections for vulnerable populations or humanitarian data principles
questions.l5: Full vulnerable population data protection with enhanced consent processes, data minimization, purpose limitation, humanitarian data principles per ICRC handbook, re-identification risk assessment, and data sharing restrictions for vulnerable groups
questions.regulatoryRef: GDPR Art. 9; ICRC Handbook on Data Protection in Humanitarian Action
questions.text: Does the agent protect vulnerable population data per GDPR Article 9 special category protections and humanitarian data protection principles?

questions.l1: No social performance tracking; financial inclusion operations are not assessed against social performance standards
questions.l3: Agent tracks basic social metrics (outreach to poor, women, rural populations) but does not implement full social performance management or client outcome monitoring
questions.l5: Comprehensive SPM with CERISE-SPTF standard implementation, client outcome monitoring, social audit readiness, responsible pricing verification, staff incentive alignment with social goals, and transparent social performance reporting
questions.text: Does the agent maintain social performance management per CERISE-SPTF Universal Standards for Social Performance Management?

questions.l1: No ECOA adverse action compliance; AI credit decisions affecting unbanked applicants lack Reg B §202.9 adverse action notices with specific reasons or feature-attribution explainability
questions.l3: Agent provides basic adverse action notices for credit denials, but does not implement AI-specific feature-attribution explainability per CFPB guidance or EU AI Act Art. 6(2) high-risk classification for credit scoring AI
questions.l5: Full ECOA Reg B §202.9 compliance with AI-specific adverse action notices, feature-attribution explainability for unbanked applicants, EU AI Act Art. 6(2) high-risk registration for credit scoring AI, CFPB AI guidance alignment, and accessible explanation formats for financially excluded populations
questions.regulatoryRef: ECOA Reg B 12 CFR §202.9; EU AI Act Art. 6(2) Annex III §5(b)
questions.text: Does the agent implement CFPB ECOA adverse action notice requirements per Regulation B 12 CFR §202.9 with AI-specific explainability for credit decisions affecting unbanked and underbanked applicants?

questions.l1: No fair-lending governance; no protected-class monitoring or disparate-impact testing is performed for credit approvals, terms, or collections outcomes
questions.l3: Performs periodic outcome monitoring and flags potential disparities, but proxy-feature controls, independent testing, and remediation evidence are incomplete
questions.l5: Full fair-lending governance with continuous disparity monitoring (approval/price/collections), proxy-feature detection, independent validation/audit trails, remediation workflows, and board-level reporting demonstrating nondiscriminatory inclusion outcomes
questions.regulatoryRef: ECOA 15 U.S.C. §1691; fair lending disparate impact governance
questions.text: Does the agent implement fair-lending governance to prevent discriminatory or disparate-impact outcomes in inclusive credit decisions, including (1) protected-class outcome monitoring, (2) explainable drivers and feature review (including proxy detection), (3) periodic independent testing, and (4) documented remediation actions, consistent with ECOA 15 U.S.C. §1691 expectations for nondiscrimination in credit?

questions.l1: No CRA support; no assessment area mapping, LMI outcome measurement, or exam-ready evidence of qualifying activities
questions.l3: Tracks some LMI outreach and lending metrics, but assessment area alignment and evidence packaging for CRA exams are incomplete
questions.l5: Full CRA readiness with assessment-area mapping, LMI outcome dashboards, qualifying activity tagging, exam-ready evidence bundles, and governance reporting aligned to CRA performance context
questions.regulatoryRef: Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) — community reinvestment and LMI outcomes
questions.text: If the provider is subject to the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA), does the agent support CRA-aligned community reinvestment by (1) mapping products and outreach to assessment areas, (2) measuring lending/service outcomes to low- and moderate-income (LMI) communities, and (3) producing examination-ready evidence of qualifying activities and impact?

questions.l1: No GPFI-aligned DFS controls; suitability, dispute resolution, and scam resilience are not systematically implemented
questions.l3: Implements some disclosures and basic complaints intake, but suitability checks, resolution SLAs, and scam/fraud resilience are incomplete
questions.l5: Full GPFI-aligned DFS consumer outcomes with suitability gating, total-cost transparency, monitored complaint/dispute SLAs, scam resilience patterns, and auditable reporting of consumer harm reduction
questions.regulatoryRef: World Bank GPFI (2020) — responsible DFS / consumer protection
questions.text: Does the agent implement World Bank / GPFI 2020-aligned responsible DFS controls, including product suitability checks for vulnerable users, transparent total cost disclosures, accessible complaints + dispute resolution SLAs, and fraud/scam resilience (social engineering protections) for low-literacy populations?

questions.l1: No prudential inclusion governance; inclusion channels operate without structured operational risk controls or supervisory-ready reporting
questions.l3: Some operational risk controls exist, but proportionality rationale, agent network governance, and board-level oversight evidence are incomplete
questions.l5: Full BCBS-aligned inclusion governance with proportional controls, agent-channel risk management, incident reporting, supervisory-ready evidence packs, and board-level oversight tied to inclusion outcomes and safety
questions.regulatoryRef: Basel/BCBS — financial inclusion governance and proportionality
questions.text: Does the agent implement Basel/BCBS-aligned governance for inclusive finance, including proportional risk controls for simplified accounts, agent network operational risk management, fraud/AML control alignment, incident reporting, and board-level oversight of inclusion channel risks?

questions.l1: No EU microfinance compliance support; obligations are not recognized or documented
questions.l3: Recognizes EU microfinance obligations at a policy level, but implementation controls and evidence outputs are incomplete
questions.l5: Full EU microfinance compliance with obligation mapping, controlled workflows, reporting outputs, and audit-ready evidence for §3 requirements
questions.text: For EU microfinance programs, does the agent comply with EU Microfinance Reg §3 requirements (eligibility / conduct obligations as applicable), including customer protections, reporting evidence, and audit-ready documentation for program administrators/supervisors?

questions.l1: New agent-driven channels launch with no ML/TF risk assessment
questions.l3: A risk assessment is done at launch, but it is not repeated when the agent's behaviour, channel or customer segment changes
questions.l5: Pre-launch ML/TF assessment with documented mitigations, re-run on material changes to the agent or channel, calibrated so controls stay proportionate and do not exclude low-risk customers
questions.text: Before launching an agent-driven product, delivery channel or technology for low-income or unbanked customers, does the provider assess and mitigate its money-laundering and terrorist-financing risks as FATF Recommendation 15 requires?
