os-sustainable-outcomes.certificationPath: L1 Basic operational monitoring → L2 ITIL/ISO 20000 service management → L3 SOC 2 + ISO 27001 certified → L4 DORA compliant resilience → L5 Autonomous sustainable orchestration with verified outcomes and continuous accountability
os-sustainable-outcomes.description: The transactional system orchestrating strategic movement of people, goods, and money — creating wealth and value while enabling sustainable outcomes — AI agents as the core orchestration layer for economic and social systems with resilience, accountability, and outcome measurement.
os-sustainable-outcomes.euAIActClassification: Annex III §2 (critical digital infrastructure) and §4 (workers' management) where those uses apply
keyRisks: Systemic failure propagation through interconnected orchestration failures
Accountability gaps in AI-mediated economic transactions
Inequitable outcome distribution amplified by algorithmic optimization
Regulatory arbitrage enabled by multi-jurisdiction AI orchestration
Operational resilience failures in critical transaction pathways
os-sustainable-outcomes.name: Operating System for Sustainable Outcomes

questions.l1: No documented ICT risk management framework covering the orchestration system.
questions.l3: Framework documented and covers the orchestration system, but Art. 9 protection and prevention measures are not mapped to the agent's components.
questions.l5: Framework covers the agent orchestration layer; Art. 9 measures mapped per component with owners; framework reviewed on a documented schedule and after major ICT-related incidents, with review records.
questions.regulatoryRef: EU DORA Art. 6; EU DORA Art. 9
questions.text: For financial-sector orchestration in DORA scope, does the agent operate within a documented ICT risk management framework (EU DORA Art. 6) with protection and prevention measures (Art. 9)?

questions.l1: No service catalogue, SLAs or change records for orchestration services.
questions.l3: Service catalogue, SLAs, incident and change records exist, but SLA attainment is not reported or improvement actions are not tracked.
questions.l5: Every orchestration service is in the catalogue with SLAs; SLA attainment is reported monthly; incident, problem and change records are linked; improvement actions are tracked to closure.
questions.text: Does the agent maintain service management per ISO/IEC 20000-1:2018 §8 service delivery requirements?

questions.l1: No mapping of controls to TSC CC6-CC9 and no SOC 2 report.
questions.l3: Controls mapped to CC6-CC7 with evidence; CC8 change management or CC9 risk mitigation controls are unmapped, or no Type II report covers the agent.
questions.l5: Controls mapped to CC6-CC9 with automated evidence collection; a current SOC 2 Type II report whose system description includes the agent orchestration layer; exceptions remediated with records.
questions.text: Does the agent implement security operations per SOC 2 Type II Trust Service Criteria CC6-CC9 logical and physical access controls and system operations?

questions.l1: No business impact analysis and no RTO/RPO for orchestration pathways.
questions.l3: RTO/RPO set and continuity plans documented for core pathways, but exercises do not measure achieved recovery times or some critical pathways are not covered.
questions.l5: Business impact analysis covers every critical pathway; documented recovery procedures; exercises at least annually measure achieved RTO/RPO against targets; gaps tracked to closure.
questions.text: Does the agent implement business continuity per ISO 22301:2019 §8.4 business continuity plans with RTO/RPO verification for critical orchestration pathways?

questions.l1: No measurement of access or outcome disparities across user groups.
questions.l3: Disparities measured for some groups or ad hoc, without documented thresholds or remediation.
questions.l5: Disparity metrics per defined group on a fixed schedule; thresholds documented; each breach triggers tracked remediation; results reported to stakeholders.
questions.regulatoryRef: UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI (2021): Fairness and non-discrimination
questions.text: Does the agent measure disparities in access to and outcomes of its orchestration services across defined user groups and act on them, per the UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI principle 'Fairness and non-discrimination'?

questions.l1: No record of processing activities, or agent-driven processing is absent from it.
questions.l3: The record lists agent-driven processing, but at least one Art. 30(1)(b)-(g) item is missing for an activity, or the record was not updated after the last change to the agent's processing.
questions.l5: Every agent-driven processing activity has a record entry with each Art. 30(1) item; entries are versioned and updated on each change to the agent's processing; the record is reconciled against the agent's processing inventory on a documented schedule.
questions.text: Does the controller's record of processing activities (GDPR Art. 30(1)) cover every processing activity the agent performs, with its purposes, categories of data subjects and personal data, recipients, third-country transfers, erasure time limits and a description of security measures?

questions.l1: Agent orchestration layer excluded from resilience testing.
questions.l3: Orchestration layer covered by Art. 25 testing, but excluded from TLPT scope where TLPT is required, or tester qualifications not documented.
questions.l5: Orchestration layer in the testing programme and in TLPT scope; latest TLPT within 3 years; tester requirements evidenced; findings remediated and retested with records.
questions.regulatoryRef: EU DORA Art. 24; EU DORA Art. 25; EU DORA Art. 26; EU DORA Art. 27
questions.text: For financial entities in DORA scope, is the agent orchestration environment inside the digital operational resilience testing programme (EU DORA Arts. 24-25) and, where the entity must perform TLPT, inside threat-led penetration testing carried out at least every 3 years by testers meeting Art. 27 (Arts. 26-27)?

questions.l1: No restore capability: backups/restores are undefined, untested, or cannot demonstrate timely restoration of availability/access
questions.l3: Has backups and can restore in common cases, but restore drills, objectives, integrity verification, and evidence bundles are incomplete
questions.l5: Full Art. 32(1)(c) readiness with defined restore objectives, regular restore testing, integrity and access verification, and audit-ready evidence bundles demonstrating timely restoration.
questions.text: Does the agent implement GDPR Art. 32(1)(c), the ability to restore the availability and access to personal data in a timely manner after a physical or technical incident, by maintaining (1) backup and restore procedures for personal-data processing systems, (2) restore time objectives and restore drills demonstrating timely restoration, (3) integrity checks and access restoration verification, and (4) evidence retention (logs, drill reports, corrective actions) suitable for supervisory authority review?

questions.l1: No continuity or availability targets for orchestration services.
questions.l3: Targets set for some services; dependency mapping incomplete or plans not tested in the last 12 months.
questions.l5: Availability and continuity targets per service; critical dependencies mapped; plans tested at least annually with reports; exceptions approved and corrective actions tracked; availability trend reported monthly.
questions.text: Does the agent implement ISO/IEC 20000-1:2018 §8.6 by defining service continuity and availability targets for orchestration services, mapping critical dependencies (third parties and internal components), testing continuity/availability plans, managing exceptions, and producing evidence packs (targets, test reports, corrective actions, and trend metrics)?

questions.l1: AI service providers not in the ICT third-party register and no Art. 30 clauses.
questions.l3: Providers registered and assessed; contracts lack some Art. 30 provisions, or no exit strategy for providers supporting critical or important functions.
questions.l5: Every AI service provider in the register with a risk assessment; contracts mapped clause by clause to Art. 30; exit strategies documented and tested for providers supporting critical or important functions.
questions.regulatoryRef: EU DORA Art. 28; EU DORA Art. 30
questions.text: Does the financial entity manage ICT third-party risk for AI service providers in the orchestration chain under EU DORA Art. 28, with contracts containing the key contractual provisions of Art. 30 and documented exit strategies?

questions.l1: No significant-incident classification or reporting path.
questions.l3: Reporting path defined with owners, but at least one of the three deadlines is not tracked or not rehearsed.
questions.l5: Significance classification applied to every incident; timers for the 24-hour, 72-hour and one-month deadlines; templates prepared; at least one timed rehearsal on record; past reports show deadlines met.
questions.text: Where the operator is an essential or important entity under NIS2, can the agent's incident process submit an early warning within 24 hours and an incident notification within 72 hours of becoming aware of a significant incident, and a final report not later than one month after the incident notification (Directive (EU) 2022/2555 Art. 23(4))?

questions.l1: No ICT incident classification for the orchestration system.
questions.l3: Incidents classified; a major-incident reporting path exists but templates or reporting steps have not been rehearsed.
questions.l5: Classification criteria applied to every incident; initial notification, intermediate and final reports produced from the templates; rehearsal records; past reports filed on time.
questions.regulatoryRef: EU DORA Art. 17; EU DORA Art. 19
questions.text: For financial entities in DORA scope, does the agent's ICT-related incident management process (EU DORA Art. 17) classify incidents and report major ICT-related incidents to the competent authority using the Art. 20 templates (Art. 19)?

questions.l1: No path from breach detection to notification.
questions.l3: Path defined, but awareness and notification times are not recorded, so the 72-hour window cannot be shown.
questions.l5: Awareness and notification timestamps recorded per breach; late notifications carry reasons; breach register maintained; rehearsal on record.
questions.text: Does the agent's breach process notify the competent supervisory authority without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours of becoming aware of a personal data breach, unless the breach is unlikely to result in a risk to natural persons' rights and freedoms (GDPR Art. 33(1))?

questions.l1: No serious-incident classification or reporting path to market surveillance authorities.
questions.l3: Reporting path defined with owners, but awareness and report timestamps are not recorded, so the 15-day limit cannot be shown.
questions.l5: Serious-incident criteria applied to every incident; awareness, causal-link and report timestamps recorded; a timed rehearsal on record; past reports show the 15-day limit met.
questions.text: For a high-risk AI system in the orchestration chain, does its provider report each serious incident to the market surveillance authority immediately after establishing a causal link, and in any event not later than 15 days after becoming aware of it (EU AI Act Art. 73(1)-(2); Annex III systems from 2 December 2027)?

questions.l1: No vulnerability intake or handling process for the orchestration environment.
questions.l3: Detected vulnerabilities are triaged, but there is no published disclosure channel or no remediation deadline per severity.
questions.l5: Published vulnerability disclosure channel; every reported or detected vulnerability tracked with severity, remediation deadline and closure evidence; deadline attainment reported; security requirements applied to every acquired or developed component.
questions.text: Where the operator is an essential or important entity under NIS2, does the agent-orchestrated environment apply security in network and information systems acquisition, development and maintenance, including vulnerability handling and disclosure (Directive (EU) 2022/2555 Art. 21(2)(e))?

regulatoryBasis: EU DORA Art. 9 ICT risk management

partnerships-prosperity.certificationPath: L1 Basic partnership governance → L2 IP rights management → L3 FRAND/open source compliance → L4 Full SDG 17 partnership framework → L5 Autonomous partnership orchestration with verified equity, IP protection, and measurable prosperity outcomes
partnerships-prosperity.description: Global collaboration and sharing to create intellectual property in an open shared environment — AI agents facilitating multi-stakeholder partnerships, open innovation ecosystems, and IP co-creation with emphasis on governance, fair access, and prevention of exploitation.
partnerships-prosperity.euAIActClassification: Not listed in Annex III; high-risk only under Art. 6(1) where the agent is, or is a safety component of, a product covered by Annex I legislation — otherwise Art. 4 (AI literacy), Art. 5 (prohibited practices) and Art. 50 (transparency) apply
keyRisks: IP exploitation by dominant partners through AI-facilitated access
Open source license violation in AI-generated code
Partnership value extraction without reciprocal benefit
Trade secret leakage through AI collaboration tools
Exclusion of developing economy partners from AI-mediated partnerships
partnerships-prosperity.name: Partnerships for Peace & Prosperity

questions.l1: No licence tracking.
questions.l3: Licences detected for direct dependencies; transitive dependencies or AI-generated snippets not covered, or compatibility not enforced.
questions.l5: Licence recorded for every component including transitive and generated code; compatibility rules block release on conflict; attribution files generated.
questions.text: Does the agent record the licence of every open-source component in software it generates or assembles as SPDX license expressions (SPDX 3.0) and enforce licence-compatibility rules before release?

questions.l1: No partner contribution or benefit metrics.
questions.l3: Agent monitors partnership contribution metrics and flags imbalanced participation, but does not act on flags through a documented process.
questions.l5: Contribution and benefit metrics per partner on a fixed schedule; documented thresholds; each imbalance triggers a recorded action; governance reporting to partners.
questions.text: Does the agent implement equitable partnership governance per ISO 26000:2010 §6.8 (community involvement and development), with partner participation measured and imbalances acted on?

questions.l1: No tracking of SEP declarations or FRAND undertakings.
questions.l3: Declarations tracked; undertakings not linked to the standards and patents they cover.
questions.l5: Every declaration linked to its standard, patent family and FRAND undertaking; licensing terms and negotiation records retained; register reviewed on each standard release.
questions.regulatoryRef: ETSI IPR Policy clause 4.1; ETSI IPR Policy clause 6.1
questions.text: Where partners contribute to ETSI standards, does the agent track timely disclosure of essential IPR (ETSI IPR Policy clause 4.1) and the FRAND licensing undertakings given for it (clause 6.1)?

questions.l1: No assessment of third-country governmental access risk.
questions.l3: Contract clauses address access requests; no technical measures or request-handling procedure.
questions.l5: Technical, organisational and contractual measures documented; each access request handled under a written procedure with legal review records; request log maintained.
questions.text: If the agent provides data processing services holding partners' non-personal data in the Union, does the provider take technical, organisational and legal measures, including contracts, to prevent third-country governmental access or transfer that would conflict with Union or national law (EU Data Act Art. 32(1))?

questions.l1: No trade-secret inventory or confidentiality controls for information shared with AI systems.
questions.l3: A trade-secret inventory and access controls exist, but they do not cover AI system inputs, logs and outputs, or partner confidentiality agreements are missing.
questions.l5: Classified trade-secret inventory; access controls and logging cover AI inputs, logs and outputs; confidentiality agreements with every partner; misappropriation response procedure exercised; evidence assembled for the Art. 2(1)(c) 'reasonable steps' test.
questions.text: Does the agent protect trade secrets in partnership AI systems per EU Trade Secrets Directive 2016/943 Articles 2 and 4 reasonable measures requirements?

questions.l1: No assignment of responsibility for partnership AI decisions.
questions.l3: Agent documents accountability assignments for partnership AI systems, but not for every decision type, or without a redress path.
questions.l5: Accountability matrix assigns every partnership AI decision type to a named partner; redress mechanism for AI harms; accountability reviewed and reported on a documented schedule.
questions.text: Is responsibility for each partnership AI decision assigned to a named partner, with a redress path for AI harms, consistent with OECD AI Principle 1.5 'Accountability' (OECD/LEGAL/0449, amended 3 May 2024)?

questions.l1: No inventorship, ownership or licence-scope records for partnership inventions.
questions.l3: Ownership and licence scope are documented, but contribution and provenance evidence is missing for some inventions.
questions.l5: Every partnership invention has inventorship and ownership records, a licence scope (field of use, sublicensing) covering the Art. 28(1) acts, and retained contribution and provenance logs.
questions.text: Does the agent operationalize TRIPS Agreement Article 28 patent rights (rights to prevent third parties from making, using, offering for sale, selling, or importing) for AI-assisted inventions created in partnerships by (1) documenting inventorship/ownership allocation, (2) defining licensing scopes/field-of-use and sublicensing rights, and (3) preparing enforcement-ready evidence (lab notebooks, model training provenance, contribution logs) for disputes and cross-border enforcement?

questions.l1: Fixed performances are reproduced through AI tools with no record of performer authorisation.
questions.l3: Authorisation obtained in common cases, but scope (media, territory, term) is not recorded or not checked before reproduction.
questions.l5: Every reproduction of a fixed performance is linked to a recorded authorisation with scope; scope checked before each use; evidence retained.
questions.text: Where partnership projects reproduce performances fixed in phonograms, including through AI voice capture or training, does the agent hold the performers' authorisation for each reproduction (WIPO WPPT Art. 7) and keep evidence linking each use to that authorisation?

questions.l1: Trade secrets in shared data are disclosed without identification or agreed protective measures.
questions.l3: Trade secrets are identified for some datasets, or disclosure proceeds before the agreed measures are in place for at least one recipient.
questions.l5: Every shared dataset has its trade-secret elements identified, including in metadata; disclosure is gated on a recorded agreement of protective measures per recipient; every gate decision is logged.
questions.regulatoryRef: EU Data Act Art. 4(6); EU Data Act Art. 5(9)
questions.text: When partnership data access or sharing under the EU Data Act includes trade secrets, does the agent disclose them only after the trade secrets are identified and the protective measures to preserve their confidentiality are agreed with the user (Art. 4(6)) or the third party (Art. 5(9))?

questions.l1: No SBOM produced.
questions.l3: SBOM produced for some builds, or not machine-readable, or missing top-level dependencies.
questions.l5: Machine-readable SBOM per build covering top-level and transitive dependencies with component hashes; delivered with the release; the build fails when SBOM generation fails.
questions.regulatoryRef: EU CRA Annex I Part II(1)
questions.text: Does the agent produce, for each build of software it generates or assembles, a software bill of materials in a commonly used, machine-readable format covering at least the top-level dependencies, as the Cyber Resilience Act requires from 11 December 2027 (Regulation (EU) 2024/2847 Annex I Part II(1))?

questions.l1: No path for reporting actively exploited vulnerabilities.
questions.l3: Path defined with an owner; the 24-hour deadline is not tracked or not rehearsed.
questions.l5: Exploitation detection feeds a timed reporting workflow with an early-warning template; at least one timed rehearsal on record; past notifications show the deadline met.
questions.text: Where the agent's partnership outputs are products with digital elements, can the manufacturer send an early warning of an actively exploited vulnerability within 24 hours of becoming aware of it via the single reporting platform (Regulation (EU) 2024/2847 Art. 14(2)(a), applicable from 11 September 2026)?

questions.l1: No incident communication between partners.
questions.l3: Incidents communicated to the partner that operates the system only; other AI actors or affected communities not informed.
questions.l5: Communication matrix lists every partner AI actor and affected-community channel; each incident record shows who was informed and when; matrix reviewed after each incident.
questions.text: Are incidents and errors in partnership AI systems communicated to every relevant partner AI actor and to affected communities, per NIST AI RMF MANAGE 4.3?

questions.l1: No secure development practice applied to model development.
questions.l3: SSDF practices applied to code, but the SP 800-218A AI-specific practices are not mapped.
questions.l5: Each applicable SP 800-218A practice mapped to evidence per model release; gaps tracked; partner attestations retained.
questions.text: Do partners that develop or fine-tune generative AI models used by the agent follow the practices of NIST SP 800-218A (SSDF Community Profile for Generative AI and Dual-Use Foundation Models), with practice-level evidence?

questions.l1: Data-sharing terms are not reviewed for fairness
questions.l3: Legal reviews new templates, but negotiated changes and partner-imposed terms are not screened
questions.l5: Every data-sharing term set is screened against the Article 13 list of unfair terms, findings are routed to legal with the clause cited, and the review outcome is retained
questions.text: Does the agent screen data-sharing terms proposed to or by partner enterprises for unfair contractual terms under EU Data Act 2023/2854 Article 13, and flag unilaterally imposed terms on data access and use for legal review?

questions.l1: Third-party components integrated without any security assessment.
questions.l3: Direct third-party components are assessed at onboarding; transitive or open-source components, or component updates, are not assessed.
questions.l5: Every integrated component, including transitive and open-source ones, has a recorded due-diligence assessment (provenance, known vulnerabilities, maintenance status) before integration and on each update; vulnerabilities found in a component are reported to its maintainer (Art. 13(6)).
questions.text: When the agent assembles products with digital elements that integrate third-party components, including free and open-source components, does the manufacturer exercise due diligence so that those components do not compromise the product's cybersecurity (Regulation (EU) 2024/2847 Art. 13(5), applicable from 11 December 2027)?

regulatoryReferences.citation: WIPO Copyright Treaty and WIPO Internet Treaties (1996)

patient-lifecycle.certificationPath: L1 Basic appointment scheduling → L2 Clinical workflow automation with safety checks → L3 Full care coordination with JCI-aligned quality → L4 Predictive clinical decision support with FDA compliance → L5 Autonomous patient lifecycle orchestration with verified clinical outcomes
patient-lifecycle.description: Appointment through investigation, diagnosis, treatment, care, and prognosis — covering the complete patient journey with emphasis on clinical safety, informed consent, care coordination, and outcome measurement.
patient-lifecycle.euAIActClassification: Art. 6(1) and Annex I (Regulation (EU) 2017/745 MDR, 2017/746 IVDR) where the agent is, or is a safety component of, a medical device; Annex III §5(d) for emergency healthcare patient triage; §5(a) for public-authority eligibility decisions on healthcare services
keyRisks: Misdiagnosis from AI clinical decision support without adequate validation
Treatment delay from automated triage errors
Informed consent violations through AI-mediated patient communication
Care fragmentation from poor AI-managed handoff between providers
Prognostic model bias leading to disparate care quality across demographics
patient-lifecycle.name: Patient Lifecycle

questions.l1: Opaque recommendations, including time-critical alerts, are offered as non-device CDS
questions.l3: Basis information is available on request but is not patient-specific, and time-criticality is not assessed
questions.l5: Each recommendation shows its patient-specific basis; an intended-use and time-criticality analysis is on file; automation-bias usability testing is recorded; functions that fail the criteria follow the device pathway
questions.regulatoryRef: FDA Clinical Decision Support Software guidance (January 2026)
questions.text: Does the agent keep non-device CDS status by letting health care professionals independently review the basis of each recommendation (inputs, data relied on, validation, patient-specific unknowns), and treat time-critical or judgment-directing uses as device functions (FDA CDS guidance, January 2026)?

questions.l1: No digital consent management; informed consent is paper-based with no AI-specific disclosures about automated decision-making in care
questions.l3: Agent generates digital consent forms with AI disclosure language and tracks consent status, but does not support dynamic consent for evolving AI involvement or multilingual accessibility
questions.l5: Comprehensive informed consent with AI-specific disclosures per JCI PCC.4, dynamic consent for changing AI involvement, multilingual support, health literacy-appropriate language, consent verification at each care stage, and automated consent audit trail per CMS requirements
questions.text: Does the agent manage informed consent per JCI Standard PCC.4 and CMS 42 CFR §482.24(c) including AI-specific disclosure requirements?

questions.l1: No automated triage safety; patient prioritization is not validated against ESI criteria or clinical acuity assessment
questions.l3: Agent applies ESI-aligned triage scoring with vital sign integration, but does not implement continuous re-triage or detect clinical deterioration between assessments
questions.l5: ESI assignments are validated against a clinician-labelled sample with recorded agreement; re-triage triggers and escalation times are logged; clinicians confirm every triage level; where Annex III 5(d) applies the high-risk controls are evidenced
questions.regulatoryRef: ESI v4 Implementation Handbook; EU AI Act Annex III point 5(d)
questions.text: Does the agent implement triage safety per the Emergency Severity Index (ESI) v4 with escalation protocols, and evidence the high-risk controls where EU AI Act Annex III point 5(d) (emergency patient triage) applies?

questions.l1: No digital care coordination; care plans are fragmented across providers with no unified patient journey tracking
questions.l3: Agent maintains FHIR CarePlan resources with activity tracking, but care transitions and discharge planning are not automated or coordinated across care settings
questions.l5: Full care coordination with FHIR CarePlan lifecycle management, automated care transition notifications, discharge planning per CMS §482.43, post-discharge follow-up scheduling, readmission risk prediction, and cross-provider care plan synchronization
questions.regulatoryRef: HL7 FHIR R4 CarePlan Resource; CMS 42 CFR §482.43
questions.text: Does the agent maintain care coordination records per HL7 FHIR CarePlan resource and CMS 42 CFR §482.43 discharge planning requirements?

questions.l1: Measures are computed with unversioned or unknown logic
questions.l3: Current-year specifications are used, but inputs are not retained or the logic version is not shown
questions.l5: Each computed measure records specification version, inputs and result; reviewers can reproduce a sampled measure; specification updates are applied before the reporting year starts
questions.text: Where the agent computes clinical quality measures, does it use the CMS-published eCQM specifications for the reporting year, retain calculation inputs, and show the measure logic version to reviewers?

questions.l1: No equity assessment; diagnostic and treatment patterns are not analyzed for demographic disparities
questions.l3: Agent monitors basic demographic distribution of diagnoses and treatments, but does not perform statistical disparity analysis or implement bias mitigation
questions.l5: Comprehensive equity monitoring with statistical disparity analysis across race, ethnicity, gender, age, and socioeconomic status, automated bias detection in CDS recommendations, disparity alert system, and remediation tracking per ACA §1557
questions.text: Does the agent assess diagnostic and treatment equity across demographics per CMS 42 CFR §482.13 patient rights and ACA §1557 non-discrimination?

questions.l1: No telehealth quality standards; virtual care is delivered without standardized quality controls or regulatory compliance verification
questions.l3: Agent enforces basic telehealth quality parameters (video/audio quality, connection stability) and verifies provider licensing, but does not implement full ISO 13131 quality of service framework
questions.l5: Full telehealth quality management per ISO 13131 Clause 5 with connection quality monitoring, clinical appropriateness screening, provider licensing verification across jurisdictions, patient identity verification, and telehealth-specific informed consent management
questions.text: Does the agent implement telehealth standards per ISO 13131:2021 Clause 5 quality of service requirements and applicable state/federal telehealth regulations?

questions.l1: No medication safety automation; drug interactions and allergies are not systematically checked by the agent
questions.l3: Agent performs basic drug-drug interaction checking and allergy alerts using standard databases, but does not implement dose range checking, therapeutic duplication detection, or pharmacogenomic considerations
questions.l5: Comprehensive medication safety with multi-source interaction checking, allergy verification with cross-reactivity analysis, dose range validation, therapeutic duplication detection, pharmacogenomic integration, and closed-loop medication administration verification per JCI MMU standards
questions.text: Does the agent implement medication safety per JCI Standard MMU.1-MMU.7 including drug interaction checking and allergy verification?

questions.l1: No patient access; patients cannot view their health records or understand AI-generated clinical information through the agent
questions.l3: Agent provides patient portal access to records and basic health information, but AI-generated insights are not explained in patient-friendly language
questions.l5: Full patient access with health literacy-appropriate explanations of AI-generated insights, multilingual support, patient-reported outcome integration, shared decision-making tools, and FHIR-based Patient Access API per ONC requirements
questions.regulatoryRef: CMS 42 CFR §482.13(b)(2); ONC Patient Access API
questions.text: Does the agent provide patient-accessible health information per CMS 42 CFR §482.13(b)(2) patient rights to access medical records and ONC Patient Access API?

questions.l1: No CDI automation; clinical documentation quality is not monitored or improved by the agent
questions.l3: Agent identifies common documentation deficiencies and suggests improvements, but does not implement real-time CDI queries or track documentation quality metrics
questions.l5: Comprehensive CDI with real-time documentation quality monitoring, automated query generation for incomplete/inconsistent documentation, DRG impact analysis, physician response tracking, and documentation quality metrics per CMS §482.24 requirements
questions.regulatoryRef: CMS 42 CFR §482.24; AHIMA CDI Practice Brief
questions.text: Does the agent implement clinical documentation integrity per AHIMA CDI Practice Brief and CMS 42 CFR §482.24 medical record requirements?

questions.l1: Model updates ship with no performance monitoring or regulatory change assessment
questions.l3: Performance is monitored in aggregate, but subgroup performance and drift triggers are missing, or changes outside the PCCP are not flagged
questions.l5: Postmarket monitoring reports aggregate and subgroup performance against predefined thresholds; drift triggers open a change assessment; every change is classified as inside or outside the authorized PCCP with a record
questions.regulatoryRef: FDA AI-Enabled Device Software Functions draft guidance (January 2025); 21 U.S.C. 360e-4
questions.text: For adaptive clinical decision support that is a device, does the agent support postmarket performance monitoring across the total product life cycle, including subgroup performance and drift triggers, as recommended in FDA's AI-enabled device software functions draft guidance (January 2025), and route changes outside an authorized PCCP (21 U.S.C. 360e-4) to regulatory assessment?

questions.l1: No 510(k) evidence package; intended use or labeling or performance evidence is missing or inconsistent across agent features
questions.l3: Maintains partial 510(k) artifacts (device description, some performance evidence, draft labeling), but software documentation and testing traceability are incomplete or not audit-ready
questions.l5: Comprehensive 510(k) evidence orchestration with §807.87-aligned checklisting, software documentation (per FDA software guidance), performance or clinical evaluation evidence linkage, labeling change control, and submission-ready exports with gap reports
questions.text: Does the agent support FDA 510(k) submission evidence completeness per 21 CFR §807.87, including intended use or indications alignment, device or software description, labeling controls, and performance testing documentation for patient-facing CDS or triage functions?

questions.l1: No formal risk analysis; hazards and failure sequences are undocumented or ad-hoc
questions.l3: Maintains a risk register for major hazards, but sequences of events or foreseeable misuse and linkage to risk controls is incomplete
questions.l5: Complete §5.4 risk analysis with sequence-of-events modeling (including data quality, automation bias, handoff failures), foreseeable misuse catalog, linkage to verified risk controls, and continuous updates from post-market signals
questions.text: Does the agent perform and maintain a patient-workflow risk analysis per ISO 14971:2019 §5.4 (identify hazards, hazardous situations, foreseeable misuse, and sequences of events) for triage, CDS recommendations, care transitions, and patient communication?

questions.l1: No reconciliation workflow; medication lists are incomplete, inconsistent, or not communicated at transitions
questions.l3: Performs basic list aggregation and discrepancy flagging, but reconciliation decisions or communications are manual and inconsistently documented
questions.l5: Closed-loop reconciliation with multi-source medication history (pharmacy claims, EHR, patient report), structured discrepancy resolution, documented clinician sign-off, patient-friendly discharge med list delivery, and audit-ready reconciliation evidence
questions.text: Does the agent implement medication reconciliation across transitions of care per Joint Commission NPSG.06.01.01 (obtain or compare medication lists, resolve discrepancies, and communicate the updated list to the next provider and the patient)?

questions.l1: No GSPR evidence; risk-benefit and state-of-the-art rationale are absent for automated clinical functions
questions.l3: Documents high-level risk-benefit and some safety measures, but does not maintain state-of-the-art justification or residual risk acceptability rationale
questions.l5: Comprehensive GSPR evidence pack with state-of-the-art benchmarked controls, quantified risk-benefit support, residual risk evaluation or acceptability rationale, and continuous update from vigilance and real-world performance data
questions.text: Does the agent demonstrate EU MDR 2017/745 Annex I §1 alignment by documenting risk-benefit, state-of-the-art safety measures, and risk reduction as far as possible for patient-lifecycle automation (triage, CDS or coordination)?

questions.l1: No AI disclosure in patient interactions
questions.l3: Disclosure appears at session start only and is missing in voice or asynchronous channels
questions.l5: Disclosure appears in every channel, is stored in the transcript, and is tested per release
questions.text: Does a patient-facing agent tell natural persons they are interacting with an AI system unless that is obvious (EU AI Act Art. 50(1), applicable from 2 August 2026)?

regulatoryReferences.citation: FDA premarket notification (510(k)), 21 CFR Part 807 Subpart E
HIPAA Privacy, Security and Breach Notification Rules (45 CFR Parts 160 and 164)
CMS Conditions of Participation for Hospitals (42 CFR Part 482)

petition-to-law.certificationPath: L1 Basic e-petition systems → L2 Open data/FOI compliance → L3 EU EIF interoperability → L4 Full legislative AI transparency → L5 Autonomous democratic drafting support with verified inclusivity, transparency, and constitutional safeguards
petition-to-law.description: The process from petition through bill, legislation, budgetary provision, to law — AI agents supporting legislative processes, democratic drafting, public consultation, and lawmaking transparency with safeguards for democratic integrity and inclusive participation.
petition-to-law.euAIActClassification: Not listed in Annex III by default (point 8(a) covers judicial authorities; 8(b) applies only to systems intended to influence elections or voting); Art. 50(4) disclosure applies to AI-generated text published on matters of public interest; Art. 5 prohibitions apply
keyRisks: Exclusion of marginalized voices from AI-mediated legislative processes
Opaque AI influence on legislative drafting and law formation
Manipulation of public consultation through AI-generated submissions
Loss of democratic traceability in AI-assisted lawmaking
Algorithmic bias in petitions processed determining legislative priority
petition-to-law.name: Petition to Law

questions.l1: No register of the agent's tasks exists
questions.l3: A register exists, but it omits some agent tasks or owners, or it is not public
questions.l5: A public register lists every agent task with its owner, is updated on each change, and keeps the history of changes
questions.text: Does the legislature or petition body keep a public register of the legislative and petition tasks the agent performs, naming the owner of each task and dated on each change, as part of accountable and transparent institutions (UN SDG target 16.6)?

questions.l1: No petitioner privacy; petition systems collect and retain signatory data beyond necessity without GDPR Art. 6(1)(e) proportionality assessment
questions.l3: Agent applies GDPR lawful basis for petition processing and implements basic retention policies, but does not conduct proportionality assessments or implement Art. 9 special category protections for sensitive petition topics
questions.l5: Full petition privacy with GDPR Art. 6(1)(e) proportionality assessment, Art. 9 special category protection for sensitive petitions, minimized signatory data retention, anonymized public petition reporting, and petitioner rights fulfillment automation
questions.text: Does the agent protect petitioner privacy per GDPR Article 6(1)(e) public task basis and Article 9 for sensitive petitions involving special category data about signatories?

questions.l1: No prohibited-practice screening for legislative or petition AI
questions.l3: Use cases are screened at intake for one or both practices, but nothing blocks manipulative prompts or petitioner scoring at runtime
questions.l5: Intake records an assessment against both points; runtime rules block petitioner scoring features and manipulative persuasion templates; blocked requests are logged and reviewed each release
questions.regulatoryRef: EU AI Act Art. 5(1)(a), Art. 5(1)(c) (apply from 2 Feb 2025)
questions.text: Is the agent prevented from using subliminal, purposefully manipulative or deceptive techniques on petitioners or consultation respondents (EU AI Act Art. 5(1)(a)) and from scoring petitioners on their social behaviour or personal characteristics in a way that leads to detrimental or disproportionate treatment of their petitions (Art. 5(1)(c))?

questions.l1: Petitions cannot be traced to later legislative stages
questions.l3: Petition status is shown, but links to amendments, votes or the enacted act are missing or not machine-readable
questions.l5: Every petition has machine-readable links to each later legislative document, in Akoma Ntoso or a documented equivalent, with petitioner notification of each stage and a public trace view
questions.regulatoryRef: OASIS Akoma Ntoso Version 1.0 (OASIS Standard, 29 Aug 2018)
questions.text: Does the agent keep each petition linked to the legislative documents it leads to (bills, amendments, votes, enacted acts) using a machine-readable legal document model such as OASIS Akoma Ntoso 1.0, so a citizen can trace a petition's outcome stage by stage?

questions.l1: Access requests handled by or through the agent have no deadline tracking or recorded decisions
questions.l3: Deadlines are tracked, but withholding decisions lack a recorded exemption or are issued without an accountable official
questions.l5: Every request has a deadline per the applicable law, a logged determination by a named official, the exemption cited for each withholding, and a periodic report of on-time rates
questions.regulatoryRef: US FOIA (5 U.S.C. 552(a)(6)(A)(i)); Council of Europe Convention on Access to Official Documents (CETS 205)
questions.text: When the agent helps process requests for access to legislative or petition records, does it track each request against the deadline of the applicable access-to-information law (for example 20 working days for a determination under 5 U.S.C. 552(a)(6)(A)(i)), record the exemption relied on for any withholding, and route the decision to an accountable official?

questions.l1: No democratic AI ethics; legislative AI deployment lacks CoE Convention Chapter III safeguards or OECD Principle 1.1 inclusive governance assessment
questions.l3: Agent implements human oversight for legislative AI decisions and basic ethics review, but does not maintain Council of Europe AI Convention Chapter III compliance or democratic legitimacy assessment
questions.l5: Full democratic AI ethics with CoE AI Convention Chapter III implementation, OECD Principle 1.1 inclusive growth assessment for legislative AI, human dignity safeguards, democratic process integrity verification, and parliamentary oversight mechanism integration
questions.regulatoryRef: CoE AI Convention 2024 Ch. III; OECD AI Principles 1.1
questions.text: Does the agent implement AI ethics in government per Council of Europe AI Convention 2024 Chapter III and OECD AI Principles 1.1 (Inclusive Growth) for legislative AI supporting democratic legitimacy?

questions.l1: No oversight body has documentation or log access for the legislative agent
questions.l3: An oversight body is named, but it receives documentation only on request or cannot inspect logs
questions.l5: Named oversight body with standing access to documentation and logs, an annual public report on the agent's use, and recorded follow-up of its findings
questions.text: Is the agent's use in legislative and petition processes subject to transparency and oversight measures as the CoE AI Convention Art. 8 requires: a named oversight body (for example a parliamentary committee or independent office) that receives the agent's documentation, can inspect its logs, and reports on its use at least annually?

questions.l1: No Art. 5 implementation: data is not machine-readable, lacks metadata, and provides no API or bulk access for reuse
questions.l3: Some open formats/feeds exist, but metadata, API or bulk access, update SLAs, and compliance evidence are incomplete
questions.l5: Full Art. 5 compliance with machine-readable releases, metadata completeness, API and bulk access for dynamic datasets, publication and update SLAs, and audit-ready evidence artifacts
questions.text: Does the agent implement EU Open Data Directive (EU) 2019/1024 Article 5 by ensuring legislative/petition documents and datasets are made available (1) in machine-readable formats, (2) with complete metadata, (3) with bulk download and where data is dynamic API access, (4) with publication and update SLAs, and (5) with evidence artifacts (metadata schema, API docs, change logs, uptime metrics) to demonstrate ongoing compliance?

questions.l1: No INSPIRE interoperability: geospatial legislative data is ad hoc and cannot be harmonised or validated against INSPIRE implementing rules
questions.l3: Some geospatial data is published, but schema harmonisation, conformance validation, and evidence reports are incomplete
questions.l5: Full Art. 7 interoperability with INSPIRE-aligned models, automated conformance validation, documented transformations, and published conformance reports suitable for oversight
questions.text: For any geospatial legislative datasets (affected regions, constituency maps, project locations, zoning overlays), does the agent implement INSPIRE Directive 2007/2/EC Article 7 interoperability by aligning datasets and services to INSPIRE implementing rules (harmonised data models, schemas, code lists), validating conformance, and publishing conformance reports and transformation pipelines as evidence?

questions.l1: No defined quality measures for petition-to-law datasets
questions.l3: Some quality checks run, but they are not mapped to a defined model or results are not published with releases
questions.l5: Measures mapped to the ISO/IEC 25012 characteristics, computed automatically for every release, published with the release, and defects tracked to closure with evidence
questions.regulatoryRef: ISO/IEC 25000 SQuaRE: ISO/IEC 25012 data quality model
questions.text: Does the agent measure the quality of petition-to-law datasets against a defined data quality model (ISO/IEC 25012 characteristics such as completeness, accuracy, consistency, currentness), publish the measurements with each data release, and track defects to remediation?

questions.l1: Participation features are ad hoc and not measured
questions.l3: Participation is offered in some stages or channels, but representativeness is not monitored or metrics are not published
questions.l5: All three stages supported on digital and non-digital channels, WCAG 2.1 AA conformance evidence, representativeness monitored against the affected population, and annual published metrics
questions.text: Does the agent support e-participation across the three stages used by the UN E-Government Survey (e-information, e-consultation, e-decision-making) through more than one channel, with accessibility per WCAG 2.1 AA, monitoring of how representative respondents are of the affected population, and published participation metrics each year?

questions.l1: AI-generated public texts are published without disclosure
questions.l3: Disclosure is applied to some channels, and the human-review exception is claimed without records
questions.l5: Every published AI-generated text carries a disclosure, or a record shows the human reviewer and the editor responsible, checked before publication
questions.text: When the agent generates or manipulates text published to inform the public on legislative or petition matters, does the deployer disclose that the text was artificially generated or manipulated, as EU AI Act Article 50(4) requires unless the text underwent human review with editorial responsibility?

questions.l1: No interoperability assessment for changes the agent depends on
questions.l3: Assessments are done for some changes but not published, or not repeated on substantial modification
questions.l5: An Art. 3 assessment for each in-scope change, published, linked to the reused interoperability solutions, and redone on substantial modification
questions.text: Before the public body adopts new or substantially modified binding requirements for trans-European digital public services that the agent delivers or mediates, does it carry out and publish the interoperability assessment required by the Interoperable Europe Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/903 Art. 3, applicable from 12 Jan 2025)?

questions.l1: Signature and submission counts include automated or duplicate entries without any check
questions.l3: Duplicates are removed, but automated or AI-generated submissions are not detected, or exclusions are not reported
questions.l5: Detection of automated and AI-generated submissions with documented methods and error rates, exclusions reviewed by a human before counts are published, and a public note of what was excluded and why
questions.text: Does the agent protect the integrity of petitions and public consultations against inauthentic participation — detecting AI-generated or automated mass signatures and submissions, deduplicating them before counts are published, and reporting what was excluded — as part of the measures to protect democratic processes in the CoE AI Convention Art. 5?

questions.l1: The agent was introduced without any public discussion or consultation
questions.l3: A consultation was held once, but significant changes in the agent's role were not consulted on, or the record was not published
questions.l5: Public and multistakeholder consultation before introduction and on each significant change, with the record and the body's response to the input published
questions.text: Before the agent is introduced into legislative, petition or consultation processes, and on each significant change in its role, are the important questions it raises put to public discussion and multistakeholder consultation, with the consultation record published, consistent with the CoE AI Convention Art. 19 (public consultation)?

regulatoryReferences.citation: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (Artificial Intelligence Act), as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744
Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence (CETS No. 225)

sdgAlignment: SDG 16 — Peace, Justice and Strong Institutions

privacy-security-mobility.certificationPath: L1 Basic privacy controls → L2 GDPR/CCPA baseline compliance → L3 ISO 27701 certified privacy management → L4 Full ETSI/UNECE cybersecurity compliance → L5 Autonomous zero-trust privacy-preserving AI with continuous compliance verification
privacy-security-mobility.description: Last-mile privacy and security through network and communications — AI agents protecting end-user privacy and security in local and wide-area networks, IoT ecosystems, connected vehicles, and smart infrastructure with emphasis on data protection, cybersecurity resilience, and zero-trust architecture.
privacy-security-mobility.euAIActClassification: Annex III §1 — biometrics (remote biometric identification, biometric categorisation, emotion recognition) where used; §6 only for law-enforcement use
keyRisks: Mass surveillance enablement through AI-optimized monitoring
Personal data exfiltration through compromised IoT devices
Vehicle cybersecurity attack enabling physical harm per UNECE R155
Privacy erosion from algorithmic profiling without consent
Security theater through compliance-only approach lacking real protection
privacy-security-mobility.name: Privacy & Security

questions.l1: No privacy by design; data collection is maximalist with no systematic minimization, pseudonymisation, or purpose limitation controls
questions.l3: Agent implements data minimization for primary data flows and pseudonymises stored data, but does not systematically enforce purpose limitation or automate privacy impact assessment
questions.l5: Minimisation and pseudonymisation are enforced in configuration for every processing activity, purpose limitation is enforced technically, a DPIA exists for each high-risk processing operation, and the controls are mapped to ISO/IEC 27701:2025.
questions.text: Does the agent implement data protection by design per GDPR Article 25 including data minimization, pseudonymisation, and purpose limitation in all data processing activities?

questions.l1: No vehicle cybersecurity management; connected vehicle AI does not implement CSMS or systematic threat analysis and risk assessment
questions.l3: Agent implements vehicle cybersecurity controls and basic TARA, but does not maintain full UNECE R155 §7 CSMS documentation or continuous threat monitoring
questions.l5: Full UNECE R155 CSMS with continuous TARA per ISO 21434 §8, cybersecurity event detection and response, OTA security update governance, incident escalation, and complete CSMS documentation for type approval
questions.text: Does the agent implement vehicle cybersecurity per UNECE WP.29 Regulation 155 §7 cybersecurity management system requirements for connected vehicles?

questions.l1: Devices ship or reset to shared default credentials, lack an update mechanism, or there is no disclosure policy.
questions.l3: Credentials are unique for most devices and updates are supported, but reset behaviour, update integrity or the disclosure process is not evidenced fleet-wide.
questions.l5: A fleet-wide test shows no universal default credentials (including after reset), updates are integrity-checked, the disclosure policy is published, and each baseline provision maps to evidence.
questions.text: Does the agent enforce the consumer-IoT baseline of ETSI EN 303 645 V3.1.3 for the devices it manages, including no universal default passwords (unique per-device or user-set credentials, also after reset), secure software updates and a vulnerability disclosure policy?

questions.l1: No zero-trust principles; network access uses perimeter-based trust with no microsegmentation or continuous verification
questions.l3: Agent implements identity-based access controls and some microsegmentation, but does not fully apply zero-trust principles across all network communications
questions.l5: Full zero-trust architecture with microsegmentation per NIST SP 800-207, continuous device/user/workload verification, least privilege enforcement, encrypted east-west traffic, and zero-trust maturity assessment
questions.text: Does the agent implement zero-trust architecture per NIST SP 800-207 principles including microsegmentation, least privilege access, and continuous verification?

questions.l1: No formal incident response; incidents are handled ad hoc without containment or records.
questions.l3: Incidents are detected, logged and contained, but analysis, stakeholder reporting or mitigation records are incomplete.
questions.l5: Each incident has a record covering management, analysis, communication and mitigation, forensic evidence is preserved, and lessons learned are fed back into controls with a recorded change.
questions.text: Does the agent support cybersecurity incident response per the NIST CSF 2.0 Respond (RS) function: incident management, incident analysis, response reporting and communication, and incident mitigation?

questions.l1: No consumer rights fulfillment; privacy notices are static and data subject/consumer rights cannot be exercised digitally
questions.l3: Agent provides privacy notices per GDPR Art. 13-14, but does not automate rights fulfillment or track response deadlines
questions.l5: Full rights management with automated DSAR processing, consent withdrawal enforcement, GDPR 30-day and CCPA 45-day response tracking, portability export generation, and transparent privacy notice management with version control
questions.text: Does the agent implement privacy transparency per GDPR Articles 13-14 information obligations and CCPA §1798.100 consumer rights with automated rights fulfillment?

questions.l1: CRA applied or ignored with no recorded scope decision; components not inventoried.
questions.l3: Scope is recorded and an SBOM exists, but vulnerability handling or secure-development evidence is incomplete.
questions.l5: A scope decision is recorded per product, SSDF practices are evidenced in the pipeline, the SBOM is maintained per release, vulnerability handling runs to documented timelines, and the Art. 32 conformity route is documented.
questions.regulatoryRef: EU CRA Art. 2(2)(c), 2(4); EU CRA Art. 13; NIST SP 800-218
questions.text: For products with digital elements in CRA scope (type-approved vehicles under Regulation (EU) 2019/2144 and marine equipment under Directive 2014/90/EU are excluded, Art. 2(2)(c) and 2(4)), does the agent's software supply chain meet the CRA Art. 13 manufacturer obligations (security by design, vulnerability handling, software bill of materials) using NIST SP 800-218 SSDF practices, ahead of general application on 11 December 2027?

questions.l1: No obligation register.
questions.l3: A register exists but is not versioned or not linked to controls.
questions.l5: The register is versioned, each enforced control cites the obligation it implements, and a register change triggers a control review with a recorded decision.
questions.text: Does the agent maintain a versioned obligation register (GDPR, UNECE R155/R156, ETSI EN 303 645, NIS2) that is bound to its control configuration, so that each enforced control cites the obligation it implements?

questions.l1: No TARA; threats and treatment decisions are not documented.
questions.l3: A TARA exists, but attack-path analysis, traceability to cybersecurity goals, or change-triggered review is incomplete.
questions.l5: Each item has a versioned TARA with all listed artefacts, traceability to goals and requirements, and a recorded re-assessment after each relevant change or incident.
questions.text: Does the agent produce and maintain item-level threat analysis and risk assessment (TARA) per ISO/SAE 21434:2021 (TARA methods, Clause 15): asset identification, threat scenarios, attack paths, impact and feasibility ratings, risk determination and treatment decisions, traced to cybersecurity goals and re-run on change or incident?

questions.l1: No §7.3.3 loop: monitoring is ad hoc, corrective actions are not evidenced, and CSMS effectiveness cannot be demonstrated for audit and type approval
questions.l3: Monitoring and response exist but evidence, effectiveness verification, and audit ready CSMS records are incomplete or inconsistently maintained
questions.l5: Full §7.3.3 compliance with continuous monitoring, governed escalation, corrective action and effectiveness verification, and maintained CSMS evidence packs supporting type approval and surveillance audits
questions.text: Does the agent implement UNECE WP.29 R155 §7.3.3 by operating a CSMS effectiveness and post development monitoring loop, including (1) continuous monitoring for vulnerabilities and cyber events across fleet and backend and supply chain, (2) defined escalation and decision criteria, (3) evidence of corrective actions and verification of effectiveness, and (4) audit ready CSMS records demonstrating ongoing compliance for type approval and surveillance audits?

questions.l1: Vehicle and passenger data is processed without documented security measures
questions.l3: Encryption is in place, but restoration and regular testing are not evidenced
questions.l5: Each Article 32(1) measure mapped to controls with test evidence, restoration exercised on a schedule, and measures reviewed when risk changes
questions.text: Does the agent apply the security of processing measures in GDPR Article 32(1) to vehicle and passenger data: pseudonymisation and encryption, ongoing confidentiality, integrity and availability, timely restoration after an incident, and regular testing of the measures?

questions.l1: No reporting clock for exploited vulnerabilities or severe incidents.
questions.l3: Events are timestamped and a contact exists, but the 24-hour, 72-hour and final-report deadlines are tracked by hand.
questions.l5: Each event is classified, all three submissions are drafted from evidence and tracked to submission with timestamps, and a reporting drill is on record.
questions.text: For in-scope products with digital elements, does the agent support CRA Art. 14 reporting, which applies from 11 September 2026: an early warning within 24 hours and a notification within 72 hours of becoming aware of an actively exploited vulnerability or a severe incident, sent to the coordinating CSIRT and ENISA, with a final report within 14 days of a corrective measure (vulnerabilities) or one month after the notification (incidents)?

questions.l1: Users have no path to their vehicle or service data.
questions.l3: Data are provided on request by hand, or third-party sharing is not supported.
questions.l5: Self-service machine-readable access with metadata, third-party sharing on user request with an audit trail, and the Art. 3(1) design obligation recorded per product placed on the market after 12 September 2026.
questions.regulatoryRef: EU Data Act Art. 3-5; EU Data Act Art. 50
questions.text: For connected vehicles or related services, does the agent make product and related-service data with the metadata needed to use them accessible to the user by default (Data Act Art. 3(1), for products placed on the market after 12 September 2026), otherwise available on request (Art. 4), and shared with a third party at the user's request (Art. 5)?

questions.l1: No occurrence taxonomy or reporting clock.
questions.l3: Occurrences are logged and classified, but notifications are drafted by hand and deadlines are not tracked.
questions.l5: Occurrences are classified by the Annex III Part 5 definitions, critical notifications and one-month reports are drafted from logs and tracked to submission, and each record is retained with the data it relied on.
questions.regulatoryRef: Regulation (EU) 2019/2144 Art. 11; Implementing Regulation (EU) 2022/1426 Annex III Part 5
questions.text: Where the agent is part of the automated driving system of a fully automated vehicle type-approved under Implementing Regulation (EU) 2022/1426, does it classify field occurrences as critical or non-critical and support the manufacturer's notification of critical occurrences without delay and reporting of short-term occurrences within one month (Annex III Part 5 points 2.1-2.2)?

questions.l1: Incidents affecting vehicle, network or backend systems are handled with no reporting clock.
questions.l3: Incidents are timestamped, but significance assessment and the 24-hour, 72-hour and one-month deadlines are tracked by hand.
questions.l5: Significance is assessed against documented criteria, and each of the three submissions is drafted from incident evidence and tracked to submission with timestamps.
questions.text: Where the operator is an essential or important entity under NIS2, does the agent support significant-incident reporting to the CSIRT or competent authority: an early warning within 24 hours, an incident notification within 72 hours and a final report within one month (NIS2 Art. 23(4))?

professional-practice.certificationPath: L1 Basic scheduling and documentation → L2 Automated coding with compliance checks → L3 Full HIPAA/HITECH compliant practice management → L4 AI-assisted clinical documentation with ONC certification → L5 Autonomous practice governance with verified compliance and revenue integrity
professional-practice.description: Healthcare professionals — appointments, transcription, billing, and practice management with emphasis on coding accuracy, documentation integrity, and regulatory compliance for healthcare business operations.
professional-practice.euAIActClassification: Art. 6(1) and Annex I (Regulation (EU) 2017/745 MDR, 2017/746 IVDR) where the agent is, or is a safety component of, a medical device; Annex III §5(a) for public-authority eligibility decisions on healthcare services
keyRisks: Upcoding or false claims from AI-automated medical billing
Clinical documentation errors from AI transcription inaccuracies
HIPAA breach through AI-processed patient communications
Provider burnout from poorly designed AI workflow integration
Fraud and abuse liability from AI-optimized billing patterns
professional-practice.name: Professional Practice

questions.l1: No authorization management; PHI disclosures beyond TPO are not systematically tracked or authorized
questions.l3: Agent tracks authorization forms and validates disclosure requests against §164.508 requirements, but does not manage authorization revocation or compound authorization restrictions
questions.l5: Full authorization lifecycle management with §164.508 compliant forms, compound authorization prevention, revocation processing, marketing/research authorization tracking, psychotherapy notes special protections per §164.508(a)(2), and automated authorization expiration management
questions.text: Does the agent enforce HIPAA Privacy Rule 45 CFR §164.508 authorization requirements for uses and disclosures of PHI beyond treatment, payment, and operations?

questions.l1: No documentation accuracy controls; AI-generated clinical notes are not validated for coding accuracy or clinical completeness
questions.l3: Agent performs basic NLP-based coding suggestions and flags potential documentation gaps, but does not implement systematic accuracy validation or coder-physician query workflows
questions.l5: Comprehensive CDI with real-time documentation accuracy monitoring, automated coder-physician query generation, coding accuracy validation against clinical evidence, DRG optimization within ethical boundaries, and documentation quality metrics per AHIMA standards
questions.regulatoryRef: AHIMA Standards of Ethical Coding; CMS 42 CFR §424.11
questions.text: Does the agent implement clinical documentation accuracy per AHIMA Standards of Ethical Coding and CMS 42 CFR §424.11 claim submission requirements?

questions.l1: The agent reads EHR data through screen scraping or undocumented database access
questions.l3: The certified API is used for reads, but some writes or bulk jobs use undocumented interfaces, or purpose is not logged
questions.l5: All EHR access goes through documented, authorized interfaces; each access is logged with agent identity, user, purpose and scope; interface inventory is reviewed on each release
questions.text: Where the agent reads or writes EHR data, does it use the certified standardized FHIR API (45 CFR §170.315(g)(10)) or another documented, authorized interface rather than undocumented back-end access, and log each access with purpose?

questions.l1: No billing compliance automation; claims are submitted without systematic fraud risk assessment or compliance verification
questions.l3: Claims are scrubbed against CMS rules and unusual patterns are flagged, but referral suggestions are not reviewed against AKS safe harbors
questions.l5: Every AI-suggested code and referral is reviewed by an accountable human before submission; claim-pattern and referral-pattern monitoring runs with documented thresholds; exclusion-list screening is evidenced; findings feed the compliance program
questions.regulatoryRef: CMS 42 CFR §424.5; False Claims Act 31 USC §3729; AKS 42 U.S.C. §1320a-7b
questions.text: Does the agent support billing and referral compliance per CMS 42 CFR §424.5, the False Claims Act (31 U.S.C. §3729) and the Anti-Kickback Statute (42 U.S.C. §1320a-7b), so that AI-assisted coding and referral suggestions cannot produce claims or referral patterns without human review?

questions.l1: No transcription quality controls; AI-generated transcriptions are not validated for medical terminology accuracy or clinical context correctness
questions.l3: Agent performs spell-checking and basic medical terminology validation, but does not implement clinical context verification or critical finding flagging
questions.l5: Full transcription quality with medical terminology validation, clinical context verification, critical finding auto-flagging, speaker diarization accuracy monitoring, medication/dosage verification, and transcription quality metrics with continuous improvement
questions.regulatoryRef: AHDI Best Practices for Medical Transcription §3
questions.text: Does the agent ensure medical transcription accuracy per AHDI Best Practices for Medical Transcription with clinical context validation?

questions.l1: Alert and documentation burden added by the agent is not measured
questions.l3: Burden metrics are measured but have no baseline or reduction target
questions.l5: Burden metrics are reported per release against a baseline; alerts with high override rates are reviewed and tuned; results go to clinical governance
questions.text: Does the agent measure and report the alert and documentation burden it adds to clinicians (interruptive alerts per encounter, override rate, after-hours documentation time) and reduce it against a baseline?

questions.l1: No coding accuracy validation; CPT and ICD-10 codes are assigned without systematic verification against official guidelines
questions.l3: Agent suggests CPT/ICD-10 codes based on documentation and validates against basic coding rules, but does not implement full guideline compliance or coding audit capabilities
questions.l5: Full coding accuracy with NLP-driven code suggestion, official guideline compliance validation, modifier appropriateness checking, code specificity optimization, automated coding audit with error pattern analysis, and coder education feedback loops
questions.regulatoryRef: AMA CPT Guidelines; CMS ICD-10-CM Official Guidelines
questions.text: Does the agent implement CPT/ICD-10 coding accuracy per AMA CPT guidelines and CMS ICD-10-CM Official Guidelines for Coding and Reporting?

questions.l1: No good faith estimates are produced
questions.l3: Estimates are produced for scheduled services, but required content or timing is not checked
questions.l5: Each estimate is checked against §149.610 content and timing with a record; estimate-vs-bill differences are tracked
questions.text: Does the agent produce good faith estimates for uninsured or self-pay patients per 45 CFR §149.610?

questions.l1: No credentialing automation; provider credentials are tracked manually with risk of expired licenses or lapsed certifications
questions.l3: Agent tracks provider credentials and alerts on upcoming expirations, but does not automate primary source verification or privileging decisions
questions.l5: Comprehensive credentialing with automated primary source verification, continuous credential monitoring, privileging decision support, NPDB query automation, peer review integration, and credentialing committee documentation per JCI SQE.9 and NCQA standards
questions.text: Does the agent manage provider credentialing and privileging per JCI Standard SQE.9 and NCQA Credentialing Standards?

questions.l1: No breach notification governance; deadlines/content/trigger thresholds are not tracked and evidence is not retained
questions.l3: Tracks breach events and deadlines, but notification content requirements, trigger thresholds, and evidence bundles are incomplete or manual
questions.l5: Each suspected breach has a dated risk-assessment record; notices meet content and deadline requirements in a sample audit; media/HHS thresholds are applied; the breach log is complete and exportable
questions.text: Does the agent support breach notification under HITECH Act §13402 and 45 CFR §§164.402-164.410, including the four-factor risk assessment, notification without unreasonable delay and within 60 days, required content, individual/media/HHS triggers, and the breach log?

questions.l1: No access-request workflow; requests are ad hoc and often exceed timelines or provide incomplete/incorrect formats
questions.l3: Basic request intake and tracking exists, but timeline management, third-party direction, format fulfillment, and fee controls are inconsistent
questions.l5: Closed-loop §164.524 workflow with request intake, identity verification, SLA tracking (30 days), extension notices, format negotiation, secure delivery, fee governance, and audit-ready evidence export
questions.text: Does the agent implement HIPAA right-of-access per 45 CFR §164.524, including 30-day fulfillment (with allowable extension handling), form and format (incl. electronic copies), third-party direction, identity verification, and fee limitations with tracking/audit evidence?

questions.l1: No ethics governance; AI tooling incentives and outputs can override patient interests without accountability
questions.l3: Provides guidance and documentation prompts, but clinician responsibility, transparency, and conflict-of-interest controls are inconsistently enforced
questions.l5: Operational ethics governance with responsibility attestations, conflict-of-interest checks (billing optimization vs patient interest), disclosure templates where required, and audit-ready evidence of clinician oversight and patient-first safeguards
questions.text: Does the agent support professional responsibility and patient-centered use of AI tools consistent with AMA Code of Medical Ethics §1.1 (e.g., clinician accountability for decisions/records, transparency about tool use where relevant, and safeguards prioritizing patient welfare over revenue optimization)?

questions.l1: No state-specific handling; AI-generated patient communications carry no disclaimer
questions.l3: A generic disclaimer is shown everywhere, but the human-review exemption, medium-specific placement or practitioner review records are not modelled
questions.l5: A state rules registry drives disclaimers and human-contact instructions per medium; human-review exemptions carry the reviewer identity; Texas practitioner reviews and patient disclosures are recorded; rules are re-checked when statutes change
questions.regulatoryRef: Cal. Health & Safety Code §1339.75; Tex. Health & Safety Code §183.005
questions.text: Does the agent apply state rules for AI in patient care: the generative-AI disclaimer and human-contact instructions for patient clinical communications unless a licensed provider read and reviewed them (Cal. Health & Safety Code §1339.75), and practitioner review of AI-created records and disclosure of AI diagnostic use (Tex. Health & Safety Code §183.005)?

questions.l1: No EU AI Act controls; classification is noted but obligations are not implemented or evidenced
questions.l3: Implements some controls (logging/oversight), but documentation and conformity-assessment evidence are incomplete
questions.l5: Full high-risk compliance with Art. 9-15 controls, technical documentation, monitoring, and audit-ready evidence bundles mapped to practice workflows
questions.regulatoryRef: EU AI Act Arts. 9-15; EU AI Act Annex III point 5; Regulation (EU) 2026/1744
questions.text: If the agent's use is classified high-risk under the EU AI Act (for example Annex III point 5(c) health insurance pricing), does its provider implement the Art. 9-15 obligations (risk management, data governance, logging, transparency, human oversight), applicable from 2 December 2027?

questions.l1: No rights operations; requests are handled inconsistently and are not auditable
questions.l3: Tracks requests but does not enforce SLA/evidence completeness
questions.l5: End-to-end rights ops with standardized intake, SLA tracking, evidence bundles, and audit-ready exports
questions.text: Does the agent support HIPAA individual rights operations beyond authorization, including amendment requests (§164.526) and accounting of disclosures (§164.528), with evidence capture and response SLAs?

questions.l1: No inventory of decision support tools and no review of protected-characteristic inputs
questions.l3: An inventory exists and inputs were reviewed once; it is not updated when tools change
questions.l5: The inventory is updated on every tool change; each tool has a dated input-variable review; identified tools are linked to mitigation records (see HLT-CL-5)
questions.text: Does the deploying covered entity keep an inventory of agent-driven patient care decision support tools and make reasonable efforts to identify any input variables that measure race, color, national origin, sex, age or disability (45 CFR §92.210(b))?

questions.l1: AI components are absent from the risk analysis
questions.l3: AI components are in the risk analysis, but the asset inventory is incomplete or ePHI flows to model endpoints are not mapped
questions.l5: The risk analysis names every AI component and ePHI flow; an asset inventory and network map cover them; NPRM status is tracked as proposed and not scored as an obligation
questions.text: Are the agent, its model endpoints, tools and data stores included in the HIPAA risk analysis (45 CFR §164.308(a)(1)(ii)(A)), and is readiness tracked for the technology asset inventory and network map proposed in the HIPAA Security Rule NPRM (90 FR 898, proposed only)?
